items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Only three sleeps to go
until the Labour Party conferen ce, and I do not know who is more excited—us, or the
Labour Party caucus—because on that day we are going to find out what is really going
to be the future for the Labour Party, and I predict it is going to be very, very dismal.
But these people are like kids waiting for Christmas. David Cunliffe cannot wait to
unwrap the Christmas presents, Grant Robert son is already nibbling on the cake in the
fridge, and of course, once ag ain, Clayton Cosgrove is not going to get the present he
wants because he is the one person who is not being named in the leadership
speculation. I do not think it is any surprise that their part y is saying that they are going
to have to get their caucus to swear an  oath of allegiance during leadership
competitions. But I do not think there is a sing le oath that could bind David Cunliffe,
because he is to loyalty what Taito Phillip Field was to honesty. So, quite frankly, I
think these guys are in massive trouble. It is going to be a very interesting weekend.
But another very interesting factor this weekend is going to be the debate around the
policy remits that the Labour Party is putti ng forward. We have heard a lot from these
people today about job creation and their great laments about what they think is going
on in the economy, but when David Parker s poke, the only idea we heard was a capital
gains tax. That is their prescription for getting the New Zealand economy back on track.
So they are focusing all their efforts on teari ng each other apart in a fruitless, thankless
leadership competition.
The guy I feel sorry for, frankly, is David Sh earer, because David Shearer is a decent
man. He is too good for these guys, quite fran kly. He is a person who is doing his level
best, but these guys just, quite frankly, do not appreciate a quality leader when they see
him.
Eleven of these people were meeting with  David Cunliffe last night. They were
wandering around the members and guests’ di ning room, looking for a place to plot.
They very rarely go up there, so they did not actually know where they could find a
private room. There they all were, all the lef ties. They were just there from the meeting
with Helen Clark. Jacinda Ardern was there, Parekura Horomia was there, Clayton
Cosgrove was not invited because he is not in the Cunliffe camp, Sue Moroney was
there, Ruth Dyson was there, and they we re doing the numbers. They were circling
around, working out how they were going to install the man whom they cannot stand as
the leader of the Labour Party.
If you want to know the reality of it, you want to read the New Zealand Herald
editorial today, because it says that David Sh earer is a very decent man and that he has
actually got a personality that  appeals to New Zealanders , unlike some of the other
leadership contenders. So these guys are really  in a cleft stick there, because they have
got a leader whom they do not support, who is fundamentally a decent man and a decent
bloke. The only alternative for them is a guy they cannot stand. And who are they going
to put in?
The fact is I do not think a nyone over there has got the gut s to stand up and take the
leadership when it is on offer. I predict what will happen is that David Shearer will ride
this through and continue as  the leader of the Labour Party, because none of those
people are going to seize their chance. That is what you have got to do in politics. Grant
is all talk, but it will not happen.
14 Nov 2012 General Debate 6591
If you are really worried, you should be, beca use when you read th is list of Labour
Party remits it is all about banning stuff and stopping jobs. So here we go. What are
they going to do? They are going to nationalise any partially sold assets. That is going
to be up for debate, so it will be interesting to see how they go on that. They are going
to ban seabed mining for minerals, oil, and gas. They want to ban fracking. They are
going to ban all coalmining. These are the basic ideas from the Labour Party base.
But there are some good things here, according to their base. They want a SuperGold
card for transport, for under-21s, and, at the same time, they are going to lower the
voting age to 16 and make Te Reo compul sory for everyone under 15. They are also
going to bring back so-called healthy food in schools. They are going to ban companies
that do not pay a so-called li ving wage from winning Govern ment contracts. Well, that
is going to be something that Clayton Co sgrove is really go ing to struggle to
understand. So when you look at what we have  got here—oh, what else have they got?
Direct KiwiRail as to who must win its te nders, and raise the ag e of superannuation to
67 for everyone, except Māori.
So if those are the ideas that are coming out of the Labour Party base—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: No, they’re coming from your research unit.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: —do you really think, when you mix that
together with the Green prescription for prin ting money, that that is going to be a path
for getting the New Zealand economy going? More important—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Show us the bit of pa per you’re reading from, J onathan. I bet it’s not
a Labour Party document.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: No, that is not from the National Party research
unit. These are your policy remits for debate and decision. There is not one idea in here
for getting the economy going. If you look at th e facts, National has got the economy
going in the right direction—halve the deficit, back into surplus by 2014-15.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Taking political advice from
“The Maestro” of Mt Albert is a bit like learning humour from Chris Finlayson. Chris
Finlayson has so little to say about the Natio nal Party that he sp ent the whole of his
speech talking about the Labour Party, and this  member, the “Minister for Cigarettes”,
the brain of Mt Albert, is content to bad-mouth Labour while Rome burns.
New Zealand is burning. Jobs are burni ng. Manufacturing is burning. Thousands of
New Zealanders are leaving, and the ostrich economists on the other side pretend
nothing is wrong. This is not about them or about us. This is about New Zealanders who
cannot pay the bills, who cannot support th eir families, who cannot find a job. As
Jacinda Ardern pointed out, they are the thousands upon thousands who have queued up
for jobs at supermarkets and fast-food chains  because that is all that they could find.
And what does this Government say to t hose New Zealanders? “You are lazy. You are
not trying hard enough.” Which one of th e 2,700 Kiwis queuing for 100 supermarket
jobs was lazy? The 2,600 who were back in the queue? Do not insult New Zealanders,
members. Do not insult their hard work. Do not insult the belief of those who are still in
New Zealand that there might be a future.
Unemployment is at 7.3 percent. That is th e worst in 13 years. It is the worst since
the last time Bill English was the Minister of Finance. It is up 74 percent since National
took office. John Key promised 170,000 new j obs. What have we got? We have got
175,000 more unemployed—175,000 people looking for work. The jobless rate is up 65
percent. Underemployment, people who are just making do with part-time work, is up
nearly 40 percent. The number of people on the dole is up—wait for it—116 percent.
Is it the rest of the world’s fault, as National has said? Well,  it really cannot be,
because the increase in New Zealand’s unemployment has been one and a half times
6592 General Debate 14 Nov 2012
that of the rest of the OECD. So it cannot be  the rest of the world dragging us down; we
are dragging them down.
Just this morning the retail trade figures  showed again that grocery spending—the
basics—is down 60 million bucks in a quarter, or nearly 8 percent. People cannot feed
their families, and National is content to ma ke bad jokes about members of this House.
No wonder the public is losing confidence in the instit ution of Parliament, sadly, and
certainly New Zealanders are increasingly disappointed in this Government.
So what is the bigger problem? Is it inflation that is below the target range, or is it
unemployment that is through th e roof? And, if it is inflat ion, why will those members
not modernise a monetary policy framework th at was written last century and flies in
the face of the global financial crisis? Why are they happy to subsidise agriculture, like
through irrigation subsidies, and wipe out th e emissions trading scheme, giving farmers
a free ride and pollution subsidies, while  jobs burn, manufact uring closes, and
thousands of New Zealanders are leaving?
We are here on this side of the House, we are here together as a team, because we are
not prepared to draw down the curtain on Ne w Zealand. We are not prepared to give up
on our country. That is what brings us to  work every day, and the difference between
this Government’s “vision” and ours is st ark. Its vision is a dumb economy vision of
basic pastoral agriculture, open-cast mini ng, and fat cat bankers, while ordinary New
Zealanders are fleeing from their country, ca nnot feed their families, and cannot find a
job. New Zealand wants a smart, green economy  with the jobs of the future that pay
good wages and build smart products and services  that people will pay the world for.
We have got nothing against agriculture— it is our backbone—but it is not enough, and
just milking a few more cows or mining a b it more coal is not going to change the
fundamental decline of our economy.
These are serious issues for serious times. They are not a laughing matter. There are
real people hurting, and it is the future of our country on the line.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Sometimes it is the little things that
happen around here in Parliament that tell us  about what is really going down here, and
so it was last night when Government member s grabbed a bite to eat in the members’
dining room. It was like watching the great Me ssiah gather with the disciples for that
Last Supper.
It begins with David Cunliffe confid ently strolling in at 6.30, smiling like the
Cheshire cat, in search of his cabal of close colleagues. He realises he is in the wrong
place but, as one to never admit the errors of mere mortals, makes quiet conversation
and exits through the next door with conspir acy all over his face. Not a minute passes,
and in come Jacinda Ardern and Chris Hipkins in search of Mr Cunliffe. We politely
give them directions and advise them that  we are signed-up members of the “Nats for
Shearer” club. They guiltily slink off through the door. Next scurry in Darien Fenton
and Phil Twyford. They are much more shee pish in seeking out their messiah, but we,
again, helpfully direct them to the correct  room. Clare Curran, Ross Robertson, and
Parekura Horomia are the next group of lost  disciples, although going by their looks I
would be a little bit worried that one of them is, indeed, the Judas.
So what are we to make of these goings  on? The first is th at Labour cannot even
organise a proper coup without  the help of National MPs.  One would not trust those
members to organise a booze-up in a brewer y, let alone a change of leadership. How
can Labour members pretend they are capable of running the country when they cannot
even run themselves? The sec ond is that the end is nigh fo r Mr Shearer. The question
now is only a matter of when, not if. The thir d is that the battle for the soul of the
Labour Party is between the “ABC” club—the old guard, like David Parker and Trevor
Mallard—and the new, young disciples of Da vid Cunliffe, like Jacinda Ardern and
14 Nov 2012 General Debate 6593

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins. The fourth is this
items.text: this weekend’s Labour co nference is going to be all
about just one thing: leadersh ip, or, rather, the lack of it.  Why on earth would debating
the constitutional changes over leadership be the key item on the agenda when your
leader is languishing in the polls and hanging on by the end of his fingernails?
But Labour’s problems are actually much d eeper than leadershi p. It is just not
credible for Labour to say it is all for jobs and then to oppose ever y realistic initiative
for job creation, whether it is The Hobbit , the International Convention Centre,
aquaculture, mining, or irrigation projects. It is not credible for Labour to shed crocodile
tears about housing affordability and then pr omote monetary policy changes that will
only drive up interest rates and the cost of housing. Nor is it credible for Labour to wail
about export growth and then propose new taxes and new charges that will sock our
export sector between the eyes.
My advice to the disciples of both Mr Cun liffe and Mr Shearer is that before you
pick your messiah, you have got to get your gospel so rted out. The real challenge is for
the Opposition to put up a united, credible alternative plan. Th e problem for Labour
members this weekend is that they are so focused on themselves and their internal
squabbles that they have absolutely nothing to offer the people of New Zealand.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: With the next climate change conference less
than 2 weeks away, in Doha, New Zealand has wilfully turned its back on the rest of the
world. We have turned our back on our mo ral and political oblig ations. We are now
guilty of our proportionate share in guaranteei ng dangerous climate change. Under this
Government, New Zealand has turned down the wrong road. We have entered weak
targets that are unilateral, conditional, and informal, and have ignored the pleas from
other countries to make a formal commitment.
We have turned away from the undertak ing of the developed countries in the
Framework Convention on Climate Change to take the lead with immediate action to
reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and we ar e repudiating a legally binding second
commitment period under the Kyoto Protocol, committing ourselves to voluntary
pledges instead. We have weakened the em issions trading scheme to the point of
oblivion, claiming it to be a “Rolls-Royce” model that can be revved up to suit the
circumstances, but leaving it with no credible pathway ahead and piling up fiscal debt
for future generations. We are missing a crit ical opportunity to m ove to a high tech,
competitive economy that promotes green investment and green jobs.
We are guilty of our proportionate share in guaranteeing dangerous climate change.
Dangerous climate change is a temperature rise of over 2 degrees, yet voluntary pledges
to date under the convention commit us to  4.2 degrees. That takes us beyond danger
territory into possibly catastrophic climate change. It invites tipping points to the
ecosystem and the biosphere, of which we have stunningly little knowledge.
Most telling of all, our two national leaders in climate policy, the Prime Minister and
the Minister for Climate Change Issues, ar e guilty of argumentation that can be seen
only, I conclude, as intellectually dishonest. I acknowledge their personal integrity, so I
call upon them to show us that this is not the case.
Let me elaborate. The convention of 1992 lays down a division between North and
South, between the developed and the deve loping world. The Nort h, in light of its
largest share of historical and current gl obal emissions, must take the lead with
immediate action in reducing emissions, while the South is allowed to grow emissions
to meet its development needs. This di stinction still applies until the framework
convention of 1992 is supplemented by a global legal agreement with binding
obligations to reduce emissions by all countries. That will be in 2020.
For a transition period of 2013-19, the North/So uth distinction still remains. Yet this
Government assures the public  that it is “joining up w ith 85 percent of global
6594 General Debate 14 Nov 2012
emissions” in going the voluntary route with our “Asia-Pacifi c trading partners”. Well,
of course we are, because most of the 85 pe rcent are in the South, with no obligation to
reduce as yet. The other 15 percent are th e Kyoto group, of which we should be part,
which are taking on binding commitments under the second commitment period. That
includes Australia. The fact th at the US, Canada, and Japan are not does not absolve us
from our own obligation.
There is, it seems to me, a touch of in tellectual dishonesty in the 85 percent
argument. There is a risk here, no doubt unintentional, of misleading the public, because
it offers a false reassurance that it is at  odds with the 1992 legal framework. We should
be ashamed, yet this Government is not.
The Minister’s highest skill level was di splayed in the House yesterday, when he
justified his climate policy by flourishing a photograph of some Romney sheep. He
needs to understand that our sheep indus try, although less emissions-intensive than
elsewhere, emits more than it should, and more than it needs to. Welshing on Kyoto and
weakening our emissions trading scheme loses the opportunity to incentivise agriculture
to be more climate-friendly. Rather than attempt theatrics, the Minister should recall the
Stern Review, which said that with 5 to 6 degrees warming, which is “a real possibility
for the next century”, abrupt and large-sc ale climate change projects estimate an
average 5 to 10 percent loss in global GDP. We  have to be wilfully blind to allow
ourselves to get into this indefensible position—indefensible before the court of
international opinion, indefensible in the eyes of the New Zealand public.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: I was intrigued by the talk this afternoon by David
Parker about unemployment. I wanted to ma ybe flick the House a few observations of
my own. One of those observations is particularly about Māori unemployment, which is
not 20 percent, as Mr Parker said in this H ouse. It is, unfortunate ly, 15 percent. One of
the reasons why we do have, and always ha ve had, a very, very large and shameful
Māori unemployment rate is that we are actually very, very young. Our youth
population is very, very large, and it is one of the reason s why we have such a high
unemployment rate, and such other high rates of low educational standards.
But I want to say that when people have a go at us on this side of the House for our
so-called appalling 7.3 percen t unemployment rate, I want to reply by saying that
Argentina, the UK, Sweden, the Philippine s, Peru, Paraguay, Israel, Greenland, and
Finland are all between 7 percent and 7.9 percent unemployment. I am not saying that it
is great to have a 7 percent unemployment rate, but I am saying that what people need to
do is actually look very seriously at the worl d economy and at what effect that has had
on our country and others around the worl d. Spain has 25 percent unemployment,
Greece has 25 percent unemployment, Port ugal has 15 percent unemployment, and
Ireland has 15 percent unemployment. Those figures show that the world economy did
tank, and it has taken a while to get back on track.
New Zealand is no different from any ot her country in the world. We have our
struggles. I know that there are other parties, and I respect what they say in terms of
where they want to go, in terms of where they want to print money and do whatever.
But at the end of the day, we are the Government, and we have to make some calls on
what we do. I am absolutely glad that we do have a National Government in charge of
the economy, because the National Government , the National Party, are the only ones
that have shown in the past  that when there are bad tim es out there, who do you call?
Not ghostbusters, of course, but you call on the National Party, because it has
experience in running the country and in running the country in bad times.
I want to also make this point quite clear. It is another, completely different issue.
There are those of my culture who continue to shout at the top of their voices that we do
not recognise the white man’s law, and in the same breath in court they use that excuse
14 Nov 2012 General Debate 6595
for their own criminality, such as the grow ing and the supplying of cannabis to our
community. This is a growing concern of mine, that people—our people, M āori
people—are standing up in court an d saying: “I don’t recognise the P ākehā law. I don’t
recognise the white man’s law.”, and it is be cause they are using their culture as an
excuse for their own criminality. I am really, really concerned about those people. These
are people who supposedly say they are leaders in our community. My message to those
people, who are no more than just petty criminals—that is all they are—is to get off this
bandwagon and stop using our culture, which is a beautiful culture, which is a
magnificent culture, for your own criminality. Kia ora.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I am glad that the speaker who just preceded me,
Tau Henare, mentioned the quote “At the end of the day, we are the Government.”, and
that is absolutely correct. Finally, a member on that side of the House is willing to stand
up and take responsibility for what is the highest unemployment this century. We have
asked questions in this House, and rightfull y so, because it is a deadly serious matter.
And what have we heard from members on that  side of the House today? Chatter about
who was having dinner with whom. It is an insult, an absolute insult, to New Zealanders
who are struggling to find work that all that side of the H ouse can do is make jokes at a
time when people are suffering.
In fact, if the worst insult that the Minister for Social Development can level at me in
the House today is that I am uptight and angry about unemployment, then that would be
the most accurate thing she has said today. I am, and I would hope that the Minister for
Social Development might be as well, but unfortunately not. Instead, when you ask the
Minister for Social Development why it is  that unemployment benefit numbers have
doubled on her watch, what is her answer? Her answer is the economic recession—“The
toughest times worldwide.” If you go on then to ask her whether or not it means that her
punitive welfare reforms are justified and fair, given the economic situation we are in,
she will respond with “There are jobs and pe ople will get one only if they look.” This is
a Minister who is trying to have it both ways. On one hand, it is not her fault that people
are on the unemployment benefit because of the economy; on the other, she is
completely justified in introducing puni tive sanctions—57,000 sa nctions used per
annum. That is double what were being used under Labour when benefit rates were
lower. The Minister cannot have it both ways, and yet she is.
There are 50,000 people on an unemployment benefit who are looking for work, and
to have the Minister claim that they are not is an insult. There are 174,000 unemployed
people looking for work who were just in sulted by that Minist er today. There are
142,000 who are underemployed, who are looking for more work but cannot find it,
and, therefore, are probably struggling to  put food on the table. But, apparently,
according to that Minister, they are just not looking very hard either. This Minister, who
tried to come down to this House and justify her rationale that there are jobs for those
who are looking, decided to do so by givi ng us a few examples. The Warehouse, she
told us, was looking for seasonal employment. Well, I used to be one of those seasonal
workers at The Warehouse. I know that thos e jobs end. And in f act when they did
advertise full-time jobs, there were 1,200 ap plications for 111 j obs. The next best
example she could come up with was New World—not even built yet—in Paraparaumu.
In fact, I understand the walls are not even up, but she was already crowing that that
would bring about new jobs. Well, when Ne w World advertised recently for 150 jobs,
2,700 New Zealanders lined up to try to get those jobs.
New Zealanders are desperate to find work and that Minister’s claim that they are
just not looking hard enough is indicative of the kind of approach th at this Government
has been taking to an economic crisis and a cr isis of jobs: the stand back and wait, the
“She’ll be right.”, the market will fix it, ha nds-off approach. For 4 years that approach
6596 General Debate 14 Nov 2012
has failed New Zealanders, and it is only good  and right that Davi d Shearer called on
that Government today to change track. Wh en the facts are presented, the Government
should change its mind about its plan, whatever  that plan is, because clearly it is not
working. But, instead, what have Govern ment members done? Well, if they cannot
improve the economy, all they can change is soci al security, and that is the injustice of
all of this. To say that all the responsib ility should go on the job seekers, who are
fulfilling their end of the social contract a nd looking for work, while that side of the
House throws their hands up when it comes to  the economy, is an absolute outrage and
it is just not right.
I know that this weekend Labour will continue to be talking to its values—that is, a
fair and just society where people get a fair  break. That is what New Zealanders need
right now and that is why they are marchi ng away from that Government in their
droves.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: After that speech by Jacinda Ardern, I
think that we are starting to see a new leadership contender emerge, because that was
the most energetic speech I have heard all afternoon from the Labour Party. I have been
waiting for about half an hour for David Shearer  to take the stand and have a go in the
general debate, as he usually does. I actua lly enjoyed watching the Labour Party last
week, because it was the most sad, di sappointed, heads-buried-in-their-desk
performance from Labour MPs watching their l eader that I have ever seen, and that is
how you know that the Labour Party is looking for a leadership change.
During question time we had the three Davi ds on their feet. We had David Shearer
trying his best, trying not to stutter 10 times throughout his questions and not quite
succeeding, trying to hold on to his job. Th en we had David Parker asking some
questions, as well. David Parker is always the professor, the poi nty-headed professor
doing his best with the numbers, but he had to drop out last time. He had to drop out last
time, and probably is doing so again this time round. And then we had David Cunliffe—
David Cunliffe, the great messiah. He is gr owing a beard again. Have we all noticed
that? What does that mean? Wh at happened last time David Cunliffe grew a beard? It
was leadership time; that is when he last  grew a beard. David Cunliffe is growing a
beard again, and I think David Shearer shou ld be worried about that. But we had the
three Davids on show, on performance, trying to show their colleagues what they are
made of.
We have got the big conference this weekend coming up, as well. Do you know what
is interesting about this conference? What is interesting about this conference is that that
is when they start to adopt their new rules. These new leadership rules are when they
start to have members having their say.
So what are members of the Labour Party sa ying about their lead er? They are about
to give Labour Party members a bit of a say in their leadership. He re we go, there is a
great website called The Standard. It is full of Labour Party members spouting their
views. Here is one: “David Shearer has simply shown time and again that he is not up
for the job. He can’t handle the stress, he can ’t think on his feet, and he doesn’t have a
solid set of beliefs to give him a firm foo ting when he stands up on issues.” How about
another one? “I should have listened to Brian Edwards and to that little voice inside that
was telling me Shearer was unsalvageable as talent. … it is that hamfistedness that has
finally been the deal breaker for me. I ju st can’t imagine how David Shearer could
survive an election campaign …”. That is what Labour Party members are saying about
their current leader. That is what Labour Party member s are saying about their leader,
whom they are about to have a say on.
And what about this Brian Edwards? What  do we know of Brian Edwards, because
David Shearer likes to say that  it is just blogger s talking to bloggers. I do not think Mr
14 Nov 2012 General Debate 6597
Brian Edwards would consider himself a bl ogger. Brian Edwards happens to be the
biographer for “Dear Leader”, for “Auntie  Helen”—for Helen Clark. Brian Edwards
was also the media manager, the person who did all the training. What does Brian
Edwards say? He says: “… Shearer is harmi ng rather than helpi ng Labour’s cause and
[so much so] that he cannot continue to lead the party.”
What else do we know about Brian Edwards and Helen Clark? Helen Clark is in the
country at the moment. Those members want to  deny it. They want to deny it, but I was
there. I was in the dining room; I saw them  walking through the dining room. I saw
David Cunliffe come through, then Chris Hi pkins and Jacinda Arde rn put their heads
round the corner. They scuttled off again, but  in came Darien Fenton and Phil Twyford.
Darien Fenton is one we should watch. She is the union powerbroker at the moment.
Darien Fenton is actually the union powerbr oker. Andrew Little thinks it is him.
Andrew Little thinks it is him, but it is  actually Darien Fenton. So these are the
members of the Labour Party who David C unliffe had trotting along to the little
meeting, and Helen Clark was in the country  too. We know what texts from New York
are all about—they are about when the leadership comes around.
Jacinda Ardern wants to say that we are joking too much. And yeah, we are having a
bit of fun at those members’ expense, but th ey are about to change their leader. But I
want to tell the House what is a real joke. Here are the Labour Party policy proposals for
the weekend. This is scary stuff; this is no joke. These are the policy proposals that
Labour is proposing on the weekend. A fina ncial transactions tax. You know, if we
cannot earn more money through revenue, let us  just tax people more. That is a Hone
Heke tax, as Hone Harawira would proba bly say. A universal child benefit, so
millionaires can get paid for having kids. We ll, I think that is something Kim Dotcom
would quite like, too. There is 52 weeks’ paid  parental leave. Not content with costing
us half a billion dollars more in paid pare ntal leave for 26 weeks, those members want
to move it to 52 weeks. They want to ban fracking, they want to ban seabed mining,
they want to ban certain foods in schools, and they want a mineral export tax. That is
not a joke.
They want to hurt New Zealanders more, lo se more jobs. We are for growing jobs,
we are for growing the economy, and that is  why New Zealanders love the John Key
Government.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere): So far the contribution from the
Government, I would say, is insulting to New Zealanders listening. It lacks empathy and
it lacks understanding of the reality of th e situation that we now face. In fact,
Government members have attempted to try to  couch it in fairy ta le terms, describing
real problems as “grumpy” and “bouncy”. Th ey are attempting to defer the problem
elsewhere by saying that we were better off than  other countries. The reality is that that
Government needs to pull its head out of th e fairy tale clouds a nd face the reality. We
live in the here and now. We live in New Z ealand. We do not live in  any other country.
It is New Zealand people who are experiencing difficulties.
As of last Thursday, the rate of unemployment is 7.3 percent. That is 175,000 people
on the unemployment roll. If you combine that with the nu mber of jobless people of
almost 300,000, with over 113,000 people who are working part-time or casually but
looking for more work, that is more than  400,000 people out of work or looking for
more hours to work. That is the here and now . That is the reality. Those are real people
and real families, struggling to make ends meet, who have children to support. That is
what we are facing, and that si de continues to treat it as if it is somehow some fairy
tale—that it is not real. I suspect that ma ny of them on that side will not know what
poverty is like. Probably many of them—and I know of one or two on that side—have
6598 General Debate 14 Nov 2012
never worked in their life, because they have been in politics ever since they have been
18. So they will not know the reality of not having a job, of not having work.
I want to make reference to Mr Henare with reference to the M āori unemployment
rate. He said that with the M āori population being generally  younger, that was one of
the reasons why there were more unemployed M āori. I think our populations, Mr
Henare—Māori and Pacific Islanders—are predomin antly younger. But that is not the
reason why they are unemployed. They are unemployed because there are no jobs. They
are unemployed because this Government is re fusing to invest in their future. They are
unemployed because everything this Government has done has not panned out to what it
promised.
Let me tell you. Do people remember th e Job Summit when those members came
into Government? We have not heard any more from that Job Summit. Do people
remember the 170,000 new jobs, which was th e target the Government was going to
set? Well, we did not get 170,000 jobs. Inst ead, we lost jobs, and now we have got
175,000 people unemployed. Do people remember the tax switch? We were told that by
giving tax cuts to the top 10 percent of employers that somehow we were going to get
more jobs. Do people remember the 90-day bill? If employers were able to fire people
easily, we would get more jobs. Do people remember the youth rates? Somehow, by
paying young people less—80 percent of the minimum wage—there would be more
jobs created. There are no jobs created, and I know that the surge in unemployment
means that this Government has not been able to keep any of its promises in respect of
unemployment.
I want to make reference to this. Those members blamed it on the recession. Well,
the recession officially ended in 2009, but th ey blamed it. They blamed it. Those are
your reports. Those are the reports of the Government.
I want to make reference to the last ti me that we had such high unemployment
numbers, which was 13 years ago, when Jenny Shipley of the National Government was
the Prime Minister. In 1999, under that Government, M āori unemployment was 14.8
percent. It was the same for Pacific Islanders. It was the Labour Government—a Labour
Government—from 1999 to 2008 that reduced M āori unemployment to 8.2 percent and
to 7.3 percent for Pacific Islanders. Where are we now? Both M āori and Pacific
Islanders are at 15 percent—15 percent. In so far as M āori and Pacific communities are
concerned, whenever National is in power , unemployment for Pacific Islanders and
Māori is always high.

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: Ā, t ēnā koe, Mr Speaker, kia ora t ātou
katoa e te Whare. Hoi n ō hei t īmatangia i taku k ōrero me mihi atu ki a koe Su’a e
kōrerohia mai ng ā kōrero mō te hunga kore mahi, me w ā tātou nei whanaunga M āori,
Pasifika anō hoki kore taea te whai mahi i te mea, horekau he mahi kei roto o Aotearoa.
Nō reirā, mihi atu ki a koe e kōrero ana i tērā kōrero.
[Thank you, Mr Speaker, and greetings to us all in the House. So to begin my address
I really acknowledge you, Su’a, for relating stories to us ab out those without work, and
about our M āori relatives, and Pasifika relatives  as well, who ar e unable to find
employment because there are absolutely no j obs here in New Zealand. And so, I salute
you for making that statement.]
Three months ago the Children’s Comm issioner’s Expert Advisory Group on
Solutions to Child Poverty released its repo rt, in which it said: “Children living in
poverty are those who experience deprivation of the material resources and income that
is required for them to develop and thrive, leaving such children unable to enjoy their
rights, achieve their full pot ential and participate as fu ll and equal members of New
Zealand society.” It then went on to say th at if we use the poverty measure adopted by
other developed countries—i.e., of familie s earning less than 60 percent of median
14 Nov 2012 General Debate 6599
income after housing costs have been deduc ted—then fully 25 percent, or 270,000, of
New Zealand children could, for all practical pu rposes, be said to be living in poverty,
with many experiencing signifi cant material deprivation. It said that poverty rates for
Māori and Pacific Island children are twice as high as for P ākehā kids, that M āori and
Pacific Island kids are twice as likely to be  living in severe and persistent poverty, and
that child poverty rates in New Zealand are twice as high as they were 30 years ago.
Although we may choose to argue, debate, or differ in the way in which we measure
poverty, I think that if  any one of us in this House wa s to sit back an d give full and
proper consideration to what the priorities of a good and dece nt society might be, surely
the well-being of children would rank at the to p, or very close to it. That is where I
would like to think my Education (Break fast and Lunch Programmes in Schools)
Amendment Bill fits. What it is is simply a proposal to make sure that kids in our poorer
schools get something to eat every day through  the provision of fully funded nutritional
breakfasts and lunches in all decile 1 and 2 schools in Aotearoa.
I hear that some social commentators like  to talk about child poverty as if it was
caused by poor parental choice, bad morals, or  poor work ethics. But there is little hard
evidence that poor people mismanage their in come any more than those who are better
off. In fact, research shows that the main causes of poverty lie else where: the lack of
jobs, low incomes, inadequate, over-crow ded and high-cost housing, poorly targeted
welfare, racism in the labour market, a la ck of education, poor  health, institutional
racism in the New Zealand police force and the judicial system, etc., etc., etc.
What we do know is that local and intern ational evidence conf irms that food in
schools programmes improve children’s educ ational outcomes, school attendance, and
classroom behaviour. We know that in 2011, ba sed on analysis of data and experiences
of national and international food in schools initiatives, the Child Poverty Action Group
recommended the introduction of healthy m eals in all decile 1 and 2 schools in
Aotearoa.
We know that in 2012, the Children’s Comm issioner’s expert advisory group called
on the Government to provide a national stra tegy for food in early childhood education
centres and schools in low-decile neighbourhoo ds. We know that with regard to the
high number of decile 1 and 2 schools provi ding food to students now, there is clear
evidence of a pressing need for food to be made available on a sustained and secure
basis and that food in schools programmes should not have to rely solely on charity and
volunteers. Depending on charity, particularly in difficult economic times, is risky and
uncertain, as the termination of the Red Cross programme shows.
I applaud the efforts of all t hose schools, businesses, char ities, and health promotion
agencies for their support. Food in schools is  a positive, practical, and simple step to
helping to eliminate poverty, and I am grateful for the broad support that I have received
since putting the bill in the ballot back in A ugust. I welcome the indications of support
from other parties in the House for such an initiative. I thank Campbell Live  for the
excellent series it did on f ood in schools, and I look forw ard to working with my
colleagues right across the House to make this bill a reality when it finally comes before
Parliament. Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: I am very happy to take a call in this
general debate. I have had to listen toda y to the Opposition going on about how this
Government, this party, is making fun of a serious situation. We are not actually making
fun of anything. What I would say is this. For a Parliament to work well, it is generally
recognised that you have to have a good, st rong Opposition. We do not have a good,
strong Opposition in this country.
I would like to refer to a letter that was r eceived by a constituent of mine, and he has
given me permission to use it in the House today. Not only is he someone who focuses
6600 General Debate 14 Nov 2012
on keeping the Government to account but also he wants to make sure that he is being
serviced by a strong Opposition.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: What does he say?

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: Well, I will tell you what it says, but before I do that, before I
read this letter, I would just like to come  back and mention something that Minister
Coleman said earlier in his speech, and that is  the fact that, actually, David Shearer is a
good man. I think he is a good man. He has done so me great things in his life. He could
be an excellent leader for the Labour Party, but th e fact of the matter is that it is hard to
soar like an eagle when you are surrounded by tu rkeys, and I think that is probably the
situation that Mr Shearer finds himself in.
This is the sort of letter that Labour members send out in  their leader’s name. This
letter is to my constituent, explaining wh at they are planning to do, on 20 September
2012: “I can assure you …”—the start is not  too bad, actually. “I can assure you that
Labour MPs are concentrating on their portfolios.” Well, they always say to start a letter
with a bit of comedy, and I guess that he got 10 out of 10 for that.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: Does it have stutters in it?

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: No, it does not. But then he we nt on to say: “We are working
on a number of important things at the moment.” Well, the comedy has gone too far
now. It has got to stop. I will not read you the rest of the letter—the whole letter—
because it will probably put you to sleep, but I w ill get to the last part  of the letter. It
says: “Labour is developing bold new ideas to grow.”—bold new ideas to grow. I would
say that a mauling by a white mouse would be  more bold than some of the ideas we
have seen being generated by the Opposition.

items.speaker: It continues
items.text: “We will be talking a lot mo re about our plan for the economy in the
weeks and months ahead.” Well, this was wr itten on 20 September 2012. In all fairness,
I guess we can say that we are starting to see some policy being announced by the

items.speaker: Opposition
items.text: turning contractors into employ ees, banning plastic bags in tuck shops,
reversing employment law change—what does that mean? Picking on poor, defenceless
hobbits? This is the sort of st uff that is being generated from the Opposition members,
and that is why, if they feel that there has been some fun poked at them, they are leaving
themselves wide open to it, because you are the Opposition—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Order!

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: Sorry, Mr Assistant Speaker, you are quite right. I would like
to come back and just read a quote here from an ex - Labour candidate.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: What’s it say?

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: This is what it says: “We’re waiting for David Shearer to give
us the Labour narrative. … Where’s he headed ? What is his direction?”. That is Josie
Pagani in the New Zealand Herald. That is what the country is  waiting for, and it is not
getting it.
The other thing that I would like to do—and I know you are going to be shocked, but
I would like to recognise David Cunliffe.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: Why?

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: Well, I will tell you why. We ta lk about transparency in this
Parliament, and I sat up there, you know, at the back of th e House—if I was any further
back, I would be in the car-park—but it gives me  a pretty good look at what is going on
in the House, and I have to give credit to Mr Cunliffe that he almost missed his question
because he was so focused on lobbying Mr Cosg rove for the leadership. I think that to
come into the House and start lobbying a colleague like that is something pretty special.
I am sure Opposition members would like to get up and talk about what is important
to them, what they are achieving, and what  they are doing, but they cannot—that is
right—because there is not really much that they can get up and talk about. But I would
14 Nov 2012 General Debate 6601
say this. Today there is something going on in relation to Mr Trevor Mallard and
Andrew Little—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Tell us a story about Borat—tell us a story about Borat. Come on,
tell us a story about Borat.

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: I will tell you a story about—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time
has expired. The time for this  debate has expired. Can I ju st remind members that when
they are interjecting on each other across the House and they do not have the call, it is
not permitted. You can interject on the speaker, by all means, but members interjecting
on each other without having the floor—they do  not have the floor—are not permitted
to do so.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.

sections.heading: Waitaki District Council Reserves And Other Land

items.text: Second Reading

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I move, That the Waitaki District Council
Reserves and Other Land Empowering Bill be now read a second time . The Waitaki
District Reserves and Other Land Empowering Bill considers three pieces of land in the
Waitaki district, those being in the town of Ōāmaru. The purpose of this local bill is to
revoke the reserve status of the Palmerston Showgrounds, to revoke the reserve status of
land in Witham Street in Ōāmaru, and to clarify the stat us of land known as Lookout
Point or Forrester Heights.
The first two matters in the bill are stra ightforward. The bill revokes the reservation
of the Palmerston Showgrounds land under th e Reserves Act 1977 and vests ownership
of the land in the Waitaki District Council.  The council had thought it owned the land,
and entered into a sale and purchase agreement with the current lessees. When the
ownership is vested in the council with the pa ssage of this bill, the council can then sell
the property. This is an issue that might well make the junior whip across the House
yawn with boredom, but I can assure that me mber that to those people who live at the
Palmerston Showgrounds this is a matter that is actually quite important to them, and so
to—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Senior whip.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Oh, I am sorry, it is the senior  whip. Well, you would never know
to look at him, would you?
The second item in this bill is the second parcel of land—which, again, the council
thought it owned, so it was a mistake on the behalf of the local authority—in Witham
Street, in about the centre of Ōāmaru, and not too far away from where we live, by the
way. The council sold the land to the current occupants. The council wishes to put right
this mistake and to be able to vest owners hip of the property in the current proprietors.
Again, when I meet those people, as I do occasionally when I am out buying bread, they
ask how the bill is coming along, because it is  something that they are a bit anxious
about. They really would like to have the status of the land where their home is and
where they live clarified. So those are the first two issues brought  with the Waitaki
District Council Reserves and Other Land Empowering Bill.
Thirdly, the council wishes to clarify the st atus of Lookout Point, which is also
known as Forrester Heights. For those people who have been to Ōāmaru, Lookout Point
is the beautiful piece of land to the south. You look down and you see Ōāmaru Harbour,
Ōāmaru out to Pukeuri, out to the north, spre ad out before you. It is truly a beautiful
part of Ōāmaru, and a very nice part of the town on a beautiful piece of land.
6602 Waitaki District Council Reserves etc. Empowering Bill 14 Nov 2012
The land was originally purchased by the Government from Ng āi Tahu as part of the
Kemp purchase. That parcel of land now known as Forrester Heights was included in
the original subdivision of the town of Ōāmaru back in the 1900s. The land was set
aside in 1885. Under a Gazette notice in 1885, it was “ ‘reserved for the purpose’ of an
endowment in aid of the funds of the Oa maru Borough Council.” Although the junior
whip for the Opposition may yawn at this point, this is actually quite pertinent to this
bill, and it does matter to a lot of people—

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: Senior whip.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Oh, senior whip? Are you sure? He is? Oh, OK. The confusion has
been whether the word “reserve” relates to whether the land has been designated a
reserve under the Reserves Act, or whether “reserve” means set apart—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: How are Jemima and Big Ted?

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: —I know I am probably speaking too quickly for the whip, but,
anyway, we will box on.
The Local Government and Environment Co mmittee received extensive advice on
this very point. Based on the evidence presented to us by submitters—and we received
some quite extensive submissions on this point from a number of submitters, and I want
to thank them for the work they did on this bill—and also the advice the committee
received from officials, the committee conclu ded that Lookout Poin t is not a reserve,
and confirmed it as being vested as an endowment in the council in aid of borough
funds.
It is interesting to note th at this issue was also canva ssed by the Primary Production
Committee as part of the Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill, in clauses 18 to 20.
In its select committee report, the committee noted that Land Information New Zealand
and the Department of Conservation, which bot h have an interest in this, had reviewed
their records, and they were satisfied that  treating Lookout Point as a reserve was—and
I will quote from the report, because I think it adds weight to the decision of the
committee—“a genuine mistake, resulting from the various meanings and legal uses of
the word ‘reserve’.” So it has been the most  terrible tangle, and it has certainly tied up
the local community for a number of years.
The Local Government and Environm ent Committee received a number of
submissions on the Forrester Heights part of  the bill. There were  around six or seven
submissions in favour and 10 against this partic ular provision in the bill. There were no
submissions against the first two provisions that I outlined, but there was certainly more
controversy around this third provision.
Also, I want to take time to thank all those submitters who took the time to join us by
teleconference, to travel to Wellington, or to write in with their submissions and very
helpful photos and documentation in aid of th eir submission. I can assure them that the
committee looked at each and every subm ission and argued—as committees do—over
every point raised. I am happy with the conclusion that the committee came to. A
number of those submitters focused on the status of Forrester Heights, on its status as
reserve land or otherwise, and a number of submissions and submitters focused on the
past, present, and future potential uses of the land known as Forrester Heights.
I want to cover now matters that were not  considered as part of the bill. Any
proposed use of the land is a matter for the Waitaki District  Council and is out of the
scope of this bill. I do not propos e to tell the local authority wh at to do with the land. It
is not the job of Parliament to do that, and it is out of the scope of this Waitaki bill.
Whether the land has been used, perhaps wr ongly or rightly, as a public reserve since
the 1890s, whether the land has under-runners and is prone to movement or not, or
whether the land should or s hould not be subdivided and sold  is not the business of the
Local Government and Environment Committ ee, and, indeed, is not the business of
14 Nov 2012 Waitaki District Council Reserves etc. Empowering Bill 6603
Parliament. I am firmly of the view that th rough this bill Parliame nt has been asked to
clarify the status of the land, and it has been asked to do only that. It is for the local
authority, together with the local community, to decide any use that the land might be
put to in the future.
I am very happy to bring this bill to the House on behalf of the Waitaki District
Council. This has been a difficult and longstanding issue for the Ōāmaru community. I
was pleased to hear the Waita ki District Mayor, Alex Familton, tell the committee
during his submission that whatever the outcome of this bill, whatever the status of the
land, he would put any future use of that la nd back to the community. I applaud him for
that. I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: The Labour Party supported the
Waitaki District Council Reserves and Other Land Empowering Bill to the Local
Government and Environment Committee, beca use we were interested in hearing the
submissions and looking at the evidence that was to be provided in terms of three pieces
of land that were being covered by this bill.  The reason we wanted to look at it closely
was that for the first two pieces of la nd that Jacqui Dean has mentioned—the
Palmerston Showgrounds and another lot in Ōāmaru—there is little or no controversy at
all, but the third piece of land, called Lookout Point, in Ōāmaru, has been controversial.
So we wanted to go to the select committee,  to hear the evidence, and to see whether
this particular piece of land was land held in  reserve or land that had been endowed to
Ōāmaru Borough Council, and, therefore, could be used in the way that it wanted. We
went along with an open mind, wanting to hear what would be said.
There were not a lot of submissions on this bill, but there were two significant
submissions that I want to mention—one fr om Mr Warren Crawford and one from Mr
Barry Monks. They had done a lot of work  around this land at Lookout Point, because
they were firmly of the view that this la nd had been made reserve land back in the 19 th
century. They believed that this land was not the council’s to be able to dispose of in
any way at all, and that it needed to be kept in reserve for the people of Ōāmaru. So in
many ways, this bill has been quite a difficu lt one. In fairness to the select committee
and the members on it, we were seeking the co nfirmation that this land could be sold,
could be subdivided, and coul d have done to it whatever  Waitaki District Council
wanted to do with it. I have to say that  we made a genuine attempt to get all the
information that we could. The bottom line is that I believe that what we were provided
with, after long deliberation and a very exte nsive search by legal people, is that the
council does have this land as endowment land; the land does not have a reserve over it.
I can see why it was confusing. Evidently, ther e was a bill that had been presented to
this House that was to, in effect, make it reserve land, but it was never passed. On that
basis, many of those who have been worried ab out this land were basing their evidence
on a bill that was never passed in this Pa rliament. I do want to commend those two
submitters, who set out to get as much information for the select committee as they
could, particularly Mr Barry Monks. It was Barry Monks’ submission, in my view,
where he presented a lot of evidence and lot of old documents that he had found
himself, that made us go and ask the officials to go back and search the records again. It
was Barry Monks’ submission that really made us have that rethink. I commend him for
that, because he was able to provide documents we had not seen before.
In fact, if you look at the whole issue ar ound the gathering of documents, I think it
was rather unfortunate because there were  documents that were missing. There were
documents that they had found that they had got from libraries and so on, and when they
went back to get further documents they found that they had been removed—in fact,
even cut out of old records, which makes people very suspicious. What is going on
when you cannot find documents, and when docum ents that were there have since been
6604 Waitaki District Council Reserves etc. Empowering Bill 14 Nov 2012
removed from the database? And so we we nt through, I think, ve ry thoroughly, looking
to see the status of this land. I think it would have been better for all the people of
Ōāmaru if the council had consulted better, and we did raise this issue with it around its
consultation. It was not good, and it has left people very suspicious of its motives.
It has also, I think, meant that people belie ved that the council was interested only in
hocking off this bit of land so that it could have money to  restore its opera house. And
there was concern that because the local member, Jacqui Dean, had been very
supportive of the opera house, somehow she wa s in league with the council and there
was some sort of conspiracy around this.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: No, surely not.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I am not saying, Mr Auchinvol e, that that is what we
believe, but because of the poor consultation,  because of the process, and because of
missing documents and a lack of clarity, people  were, rightly, left with that impression.
That is why it was important that we did thorough work on establis hing the legality of
this land. Is it a reserve? Was it endowment land? I have to say on behalf of the Labour
Party that we are satisfied that this is endowment land that the council can dispose of.
We then get to the point of what it wants to dispose of it for. Some of the
submissions raised the point that this particul ar piece of land is pre tty unstable. In fact,
there have been slips up there. They gave us photographs showing that this land was not
stable and asked how this could be used fo r a subdivision. That is something that the
council has to work out, and it is not our job to d ecide whether land is stable or not, but
that was an issue that was raised. I am pl eased that a number of my colleagues took the
time out to actually go to L ookout Point. I have got two of my colleagues who are
sitting here very interested. In fact, Mr Twyford is goi ng to speak on this bill. He made
a special trip to go and look at the land itself and to meet w ith those who were
concerned, and so did Damien O’ Connor. As good Opposition members of
Parliament—sorry, I forgot a third person. David Clark from Dunedin also showed great
interest. So we had three Labour members of Parliament, which is probably more than
the National Party. Jacqui Dean  has no doubt been there, but I am not sure whether the
rest of the National members even know about  it. But I do know we were prepared to
uncover every stone in search of what the appr opriate designation is for this land. In my
view, we have reached the point where we are satisfied.
There is one irony I do want to point out, t hough. If this land is subdivided and sold
for the restoration of the opera house by the coun cil, the irony is we have a bill before
this Parliament, a local government amendment bill, amending the Local Government
Act 2002, which says that the councils should be involved in only things that councils
can be involved in. You would have to say: is the use of the money from this land
appropriate for the restorati on of an opera house under the Government’s definition of
the purpose of local government? We would sa y yes. We believe that it is. If the
community wants it, if it has consulted w ith the community, if it is a community
decision, then that would be appropriate. However, under National’s Local Government
Act 2002 Amendment Bill, it w ould not be, because surely an opera house could be
provided by the private sector. So there is this sort of—is it a schizophrenic approach?
Maybe it is the hypocrisy approach to local  government, wanting the money from this
land to put into an opera house for a council that  is being told that th at is not really the
sort of thing that it ought to be involved in.
We do support this bill in the second reading and will support it throughout its stages
because I believe the hard work was done on this particular pi ece of land, Lookout
Point. It was the controversial part of the bill, and I think the select committee, ably
chaired by the member from Christchurch Central, resolved the issues satisfactorily.
14 Nov 2012 Waitaki District Council Reserves etc. Empowering Bill 6605

items.speaker: NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to speak on the
Waitaki District Council Reserves and Ot her Land Empowering Bill. The first thing I
would like to do is acknowledge the excellent  local member, Jacqui Dean, and the huge
amount of work that she has done to ensure that this bill is ta ken through Parliament.
She is a great local member. I did hear in some of the other speeches—and I want to just
address this—that some members have gone to the beautiful place of Ōāmaru to do their
own research. I think that is a great thing if a piece of legislation is going through the
House. Not all other members on this side have been able to do that, but we have so
much confidence in our local member, Jacqui  Dean, and the work that she has done
over several years, that we di d not necessarily need to vi sit, and I do look forward to
visiting in the near future.
I also would like to acknowledge the very competent chair of the Local Government
and Environment Committee, Nicky Wagner, who has worked tirelessly as well with
the local member, Jacqui Dean, on this bill.
As has already been mentioned, this bill deals with several provisions around land.
One of them was more controversial, as  has already been mentioned. The less
controversial ones were the Palmerston Showgrounds and the lot 1 ones, which were
more straightforward because they are a revocation of the land’s Reserves Act status. In
the case of the Palmerston Showgrounds land, th e bill will allow the Waitaki District
Council to sell the land to the cu rrent lessees. In the case of the lot 1 secti on, the bill
will allow the Waitaki District Council to regularise the sale of the section to the current
registered proprietors, and will allow title to their property to be unencumbered by any
notation relating to the Reserves Act.
When we get to the key area that has been  the subject of many of the submissions
that we have received, Lookout Point, I think it is important to reiterate what has been
mentioned by both the member Jacqui Dean an d the Hon Annette King, and that is that
in all of the submissions you can see the huge amount of work that many people have
gone into to ensure that the research happened. If we ju st go back through the history
here of Lookout Point, there was a very, very  clear disagreement, or misunderstanding,
or confusion, if you like, that needed to be resolved. The part icular issue with regard to
Lookout Point was that an administrative ove rsight in 1937 had mistakenly vested the
land in what was then the Ōāmaru Borough Council as a reserve. Reserve status and
endowment status are two completely sepa rate concepts, and this was not fully
appreciated in 1937.
We discussed this at length at the Local  Government and Environment Committee. I
want to pay tribute at the moment to th e huge amount of work done as well—it was not
just by local people in Ōāmaru—by Land Information New Zealand, Ng āi Tahu, the
Department of Conservation, the Commissioner of Crown Lands, and the Parliamentary
Counsel Office. As to what came back, there is a very clear statem ent from our report,
because I think it does resolve this longsta nding issue, after lots  of research by the
community, and all Government agencies, and the local member for Waitaki. I want to
read this key statement from the Pr imary Production Committee’s report on the

items.speaker: Reserves and Other Land Disposal Bill
items.text: “Having reviewed their records, Land
Information New Zealand and the Department of Conservation are satisfied that treating
Lookout Point as a reserve was indeed a genui ne mistake, resulting from the various
meanings and legal uses of the word ‘reser ve’. While we appreciate the sentiment of
submitters and acknowledge there is contenti on on this issue, after receiving advice
from Land Information New Zealand and the Department of Conservation we believe
that the land was actually classified as ‘re serves’ for an endowment in aid of borough
funds rather than as a recreation or similar reserve.”
6606 Waitaki District Council Reserves etc. Empowering Bill 14 Nov 2012
For me, that statement summarises seve ral years of work by people in the Ōāmaru
community, by the local member, Jacqui Dea n, by numerous Government departments,
and by the Primary Production Committee. I want  to address that, because I think it is
important at this point as well not only to say that th ere has been research by the
community, that our select committee has considered the bill at length—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: The Labour members.

items.speaker: NIKKI KAYE
items.text: —and that the Labour memb ers have gone down to Ōāmaru, I
acknowledge that, and that the National members have put a lot of faith in Jacqui Dean,
because we know what a great member she is—

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: And I’ve been there.

items.speaker: NIKKI KAYE
items.text: And Maggie Barry has personally be en there, as well. As Annette
King said, I think, we will leave no stone unturned, which is incredibly appropriate
given that we are talking about Ōāmaru.
But can I come back to some more of th e history, because I think members will be
very interested in this. The Primary Production Committee heard submissions on 7 May
2009, and the council presented to the committee at the time. This was the key part of
its report, which I think is aligned with our re port, but it says, as reported back from the

items.speaker: Primary Production Committee
items.text: “Clauses 18 to 20 relate to land in the Waitaki District
known as Lookout Point or Forrester Height s. The submissions we received concern
one key issue: whether Lookout Point was mi stakenly treated as  reserve land under
Reserves Act legislation, or whether the council is attempti ng to circumvent the law to
enable a building development.” I think what is  really important is that we come back
again to that point—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Cut to the chase.

items.speaker: NIKKI KAYE
items.text: No, it is very importan t, given that so many people have worked on
this issue, Mr Twyford, that we go through this history and unders tand that there has
been a lot of research by Government agencies, the community, the Primary Production
Committee, and the Local Government and En vironment Committee. I know what it is
like to have a local issue that is of controve rsy. What I am very confident of as I stand
in this House is that we have left no stone  unturned. We have ha d this issue go through
several select committees in Parliament. There has been so much research on this issue.
But the key, important point that I want to make is that th rough several select
committee processes we have ended up at this point where we can say we are confident
in the approach we have take n with regard to Lookout Point.  But what we have said in
the select committee’s report on the bill is that the Reserves and Other Lands Disposal
Bill is currently before Parliament, and we ha ve made this point: “We know that clause
7 of this bill is the same as clause 20 of the Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill,
which is currently awaiting its second reading in the House.”, and what is important is
that “There is nothing in Sta nding Orders that disallows two different bills from having
identical clauses.” I think th e conclusion is that in this circumstance “the identical
clause can be removed from whichever bill is enacted second by an amendment at the
committee of the whole House stage.” I wanted to raise that point because I think it is
very important for this House to understa nd that so many members across the Chamber
have cared so much about this issue that we have got two identical clauses in two bills.
We know that it is impo rtant to the people of Ōāmaru to resolve this issue finally and
once and for all. That does not mean that every person in the community will be happy,
but what it means is that there has been a very, very thorough process with regard to this
bill.
Again, I want to acknowledge the member for Waitaki, because I think she has dealt
with this issue with incredible diligence.  She has carried hers elf well throughout it. I
want to acknowledge the people of Ōāmaru for the many submissions they put in. I
14 Nov 2012 Waitaki District Council Reserves etc. Empowering Bill 6607
want to acknowledge members across the Hous e. I can see Eugenie Sage. I can see the
Hon Annette King. I want to acknowledge Ni cky Wagner, the brilliant chair of the
Local Government and Environment Committ ee, and other members of the committee
for the diligent approach we have taken on this issue. Finall y, can I commend to the
House this bill to resolve this issue on ce and for all, so that the people of Ōāmaru will
know that we have left no stone unturned and they can sleep easier tonight. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Back when I was considerably younger—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Before that speech started.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Before the last speech starte d—actually, it was a lot longer
than that. Over 5 years ago I was the Minister for Land Information. I was also the
former member for Otago; Jacqui Dean knocked me off my perch. The local council
came to see me and said it had a problem . It had a piece of land called Forrester
Heights, and it was only a very small part of Lookout Point, which is an issue that vexes
some locals in terms of the terminology we  are using around this. But, anyway, the
council came to see me and said: “We want to put it beyond doubt that this land is
endowment land rather than re serve land.” If it was reserv e land and it was properly set
aside as a reserve, then it could not just be taken by th e council and sold, with the
money to be put into some other purpose. If  it was an endowment,  if it was endowment
property, then it is treated as an asset that the council can do what it wants with,
including selling it and using the money for some other purpose.
I was aware that there was controversy around this, because some of the members of
my own labour organisation at the time, and the Labour Party, had a contrary view. As
the Minister for Land Information it was my  duty to find out whether the council was
correct or whether the opponents to sale were correct. Despite the fact that it might have
been politically advantageous for me to take a political line, I never did. I actually just
sought the facts.
How do you do that? Well, if you are th e Minister for Land Information the
traditional view is that the ministry writes to the Department of Conservation and seeks
its advice as to the proper status of the land. The De partment of Conservation has got
planners and it also has a duty to make sure that conservation interests, including those
in respect of reserves, are pr operly dealt with. If, as a basi s of that inquiry, it becomes
clear that the status of the land is incorre ctly recorded on the ti tle to the land and it
needs to be fixed, then the route through to doing that is  generally through a Reserves
and Other Lands Disposal Bill. There is a good tr adition in this Parliament that the only
things that go into a Reserves and Other Lands  Disposal Bill are things where it is clear
that there is a mistake on the title and it is not contentious.
I looked into it and I had in itial advice from the Department of Conservation, which
advised Land Information, which advised me that this land was properly described as
endowment land. Because of the criticisms and the correspondence and the personal
representations I had had from the other side , I actually got the department, through my
office, to go back and check. It did, and it found again that it wa s endowment land, not
reserve land. So way back then, when I wa s considerably younger than I am now, we
put it in a bill.
The sad thing about this is  that the delay here has had quite serious financial
consequences for the council. Since this bill has been sitting on the Order Paper and has
been mucked around with for 4 years, property prices have gone back in Ōāmaru. The
amount the council is going to get for thes e sections has decrea sed. A number of the
contracts the council had to sell sections w ill have fallen over because they will have
passed the date by which—

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: It’s all gone.
6608 Waitaki District Council Reserves etc. Empowering Bill 14 Nov 2012

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: It is all gone. All of them have fallen over because they are
beyond the point where they had to get their Resource Management Act consents and
provide new titles to the lots being sold. I ha ve to say to the National Party that I do not
think that reflects very well on this House, because this has—

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: No—it sat for 3 years on the Order Paper under Labour.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Jacqui Dean says it had 3 years on the Order Paper under
Labour. That is not correct, because I was not  the Minister for Land Information for 3
years, and it was actually me that put it in the original Rese rves and Other Lands
Disposal Bill. What is correct is that at the end of the last Parliament it was in a
Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill. Ever since then it has been able to be passed
within a week—within a week.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: It wasn’t a priority.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: But it was not a priority  for the Government. The
Government then decided it would start this pr ocess again, despite the fact that all these
things were looked into by a prior Pr imary Production Committee looking at the
Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill. It thought it would do it again through a local
bill, the Waitaki District Council Reserv es and Other Land Empowering Bill—sorry,
not the Government, the local member. I thi nk the local member was right to do that,
and Jacqui Dean is to be congratulated on doing that, because there was no other way
forward. The Government refused to bring this matter forward on the Order Paper.
There are a couple of things. The paper record of this is tortured. It is so tortured that
the select committee that last looked at it was persuaded by a submission from Barry
Monks, who had turned up an archive that no one else had turned up. Barry Monks is to
be congratulated on finding a pape r trail in this that none of the departments, as far as I
am aware, had found. That paper trail appeared to say that this was a reserve, rather than
a piece of endowment land. But there were bits  of information that went both ways, and
so the select committee said that the only way to sort this out was for the select
committee to get some legal advice on the basis of all of this pape r that had now been
found, and the full history that wa s then available, in order to clarify whether at law it
was endowment land or reserve land. Sadly for Barry Monks and the other people in
Ōāmaru who feel very strongly that this is pr operly classified as a reserve, the proper
advice is that on the balance of the evidence it is endowment land. So a decision has to
be taken. The Local Government and Environment Committee members from both
sides of the House reached the conclusion that it was properly endowment land and
therefore it ought to be sold, which, of course, was the effe ct of the provision in the
Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill as  a consequence of the process we went
through when I was considerably younger.
There is one further point. We hear this land described as Lookout Point. I know that
one of the issues that vexes some of the loca l opponents to this is that they think this
misdescribes this land. The land is locally know n as Forrester Heights, which is part of
Lookout Point. Lookout Point includes some ve ry important reserves, and there is no
doubt that a lot of the land on Lookout Point is a reserve. There are walking tracks on it.
It is not part of the land adjacent to the road, which is the Forrester Heights subdivision.
Lookout Point goes further than that. So I want  to put on record fo r the satisfaction of
those people who are interested in that issu e that I agree with them—it is properly
described as Forrester Heights rather than Lookout Point—but the legal description of
the land, which is what matters in this bill, is correct.
It is a shame that the fina nces of the council  are worse because there has been so
much delay in passing the original piece of  legislation, which still languishes on the
Order Paper. You know, this Parliament could have passed the original bill and not just
fixed this problem but fixed the about dozen other issues that are also fixed in the
14 Nov 2012 Waitaki District Council Reserves etc. Empowering Bill 6609
Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill—wh ich was going to fix similar problems in
other parts of the country—in the same time that  it has taken us to pass this bill. In fact,
there would have been a lot less waste of select committee time doing again what has
already been done. But, no, it has been chosen to proceed by way of a local bill, because
the member for Waitaki, Jacqui Dean, became frustrated that her Government would not
pass the Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill, which was of identical effect in
respect of the Forrester Heights land. She found that to advance that, the member had to
advance a local bill. It is a pity that this could not have been advanced as part of the
Reserves and Other Lands Disposal Bill.
I am sad for the people who think that they were right in terms of their criticisms of
the council. Could I also say th at the confusion that reigned in this was not the fault of
either the council or the people who thought from the paper record that this was
properly reserve land. It was a tr uly confusing set of affairs.  I am not criticising anyone
on either side of the debate. Sadly, in the end, where there is a di spute as to what the
correct state of affairs is, someone eventual ly has to make a d ecision. Otherwise these
things would just go on until I am retired—even ol der. But the reality is that in the end,
where there is a dispute, someone has to ta ke a decision eventually. In this case, both
sides of Parliament have looked at it res ponsibly and in a principled manner, have
applied the law, which it is our duty to do, and have found that this is endowment land.
Accordingly, the Labour Party will be voting for this bill.
