items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. T ēnā koutou e te Whare.
I would like to start speaking on the first read ing of the Land Transport (Admissibility
of Evidential Breath Tests) Amendment Bi ll. I would like to begin by acknowledging
the member Scott Simpson for introducing a b ill with the very worthy aim of reducing
drink-driving. I think we can all agree that this is an incredibly worthy objective. The
6626 Land Transport (Evidential Breath Tests) Amdt Bill 14 Nov 2012
Green Party would like nothing more than to see a reduction in the amount of dangerous
drink-driving that does occur already in New Zealand.
However, having considered this bill as it has been introduced, I do think that it falls
well short of the mark. It will do very little to reduce drink- driving, if anything at all.
There are multiple ways that we could approach the problem of drink-driving. I think
that it is a serious problem that the Green  Party would like to see addressed, and we
would be very happy to support members on th e National side of the House, or any
members in the House, or the Government, to this end of reducing drink-driving.
I think that the most obvious legislative change that the Government could make to
reduce drink-driving would be to lower the legal limit for al l drivers. I suppose I have a
huge question in my mind: why is that sort  of initiative not be ing taken? If this
Government was actually serious about re ducing drink-driving, surely it would be
willing to take a step that so many other c ountries around the world have already taken:
to reduce the blood-alcohol concentration legal limit from 0.08 to 0.05. All the evidence
shows it would make a dramatic difference in increasing safety on our roads, and
increasing the safety and well-being of New Zealanders—whether th ey be in cars or
not—if they are in the land transport environm ent in New Zealand. So it is with some
regret that I note that this bill will actually  do nothing at all to reduce the drink-driving
that occurs in New Zealand.
Another very effective policy that the Na tional Party, or members in the National
Party, could take to reduce drink-drivi ng and reduce onerous regulations, which I
believe they are opposed to, would be to remove  the requirements in district plans that
currently force bars and pubs to provide massi ve off-street car-parks. On the one hand
we have this policy, a public policy, that says  “One shall not drink and then drive. One
shall not drive under the influe nce of alcohol.”, yet on the ot her hand patrons of bars
and of pubs cannot avoid spending the money for the large off-street car-parks that
district councils are forcing bars and pubs to put in through their onerous district council
regulations. I know personally th at I have spoken with a lawyer whose client had a
prominent, well-patronised bar in downtown Christchur ch—this was prior to the
earthquake—and that bar, because of the requi rements in the Christchurch district plan,
was required to put in 100 car-parks. That is 100 car-parks that they were forced to put
in. It was a third of their overhead, so we are talking about a pretty substantial cost
imposed on developers, which results in nothing if not people being more likely to drink
and drive. It just seems to me that this is  an easy policy win. It is a low-cost way of
giving councils the signal that  it is actually up to devel opers whether or not they are
going to provide off-street car -parks. But particularly in the case of bars and pubs, I
believe it would be extremely important for them  not to be forced to provide off-street
car-parks.
The question for the House is whether we re ally want to legislate to address what
was only one problem in maybe one or two cases ever. That is what this bill does. It is
for that reason that the Green Party will not be supporting this  bill at the first reading.
We simply do not believe that it passes the te st of being necessary or being sufficient to
address the problem of drink- driving in New Zealand. We ar e particularly concerned at
the proposed wording in subsection (5), insert ed by clause 4, which is very, very broad
and very vague. What this says is that it is going to change  the rules around the
admissibility of breath tests for any reas on at all, even though supposedly, purportedly,
the bill is being introduced specifically for th e case of when a blood specimen is not
able—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Time has expired.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I am very, very pleased  to talk in strong
support of this Land Transport (Admissibility  of Evidential Breath Tests) Amendment
14 Nov 2012 Land Transport (Evidential Breath Tests) Amdt Bill 6627
Bill. The principal reason is that I wrote it. As members know, only one bill can go into
the ballot, and I do hope that my Financial Assistance for Live Organ Donors Bill does
eventually get pulled out. In the meantime I pass this bill on to my very good friend and
colleague Mr Simpson, who had the great good fo rtune to have this bill pulled from the
ballot. I congratulate him on that good luck, but also on the very careful consideration in
the process of bringing this to the House fo r its first reading. I congratulate him on the
excellent work that he has done.
This bill actually had its ge nesis in a conversation I had with a senior constable in
Dunedin who just happened to be my brother.  It is actually quite advantageous coming
from a very large family: one gets lots of policy advice on ma tters like aviation,
defence, law and order, resource management , law, education, health, and so on. This
was one of those conversations where he descri bed an incident that had occurred to him
in Dunedin, not dissimilar to th e case that is described in Police v Childs, described by
Scott Simpson in his contribution. Havi ng pulled over a person suspected of drink-
driving, an evidential breath test was take n where the fellow blew somewhere in the
region of 660—clearly over the limit by that measure. He elected blood, but the blood
was unable to be taken, because he was an intravenous drug user and his veins were not
of sufficient quality to draw  the necessary blood. Suspecting that the driver was also
under the influence of illegal substances—interestingly enough, an impairment test was
introduced under the drug-driving laws passed by this Government in 2009, when I was
a member of the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee. Being the new member
on that committee I actually undertook the fi rst impairment test, which was onerous.
Nevertheless, this fellow—

items.speaker: Charles Chauvel
items.text: Did you pass?

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I passed, yes, having been completely sober at 10.30
in the morning, which is the case, I reassure th e House, usually. But, in fact, this fellow
also passed, and therefore the doors were cl osed to any form of prosecution under the
Land Transport Act as it exists right now. The judge addressed this issue, and, in fact,
the police, I think, were quite optimistic in their attempts to charge this fellow with both
refusing to permit a blood specimen or, in th e alternative, drivi ng with excess breath
alcohol. Clearly, the latter is not allowed under th is bill, and that is what the bill intends
to remedy. But he certainly permitted them to  have a go, and, in fact, he challenged
them to have a go at getting blood out of  this person’s veins. I want to quote the
judgment; in fact, I think this quotes the counsel for the defence in the Childs case,
where he said in his submission that “Had Pa rliament considered it appropriate to allow
the prosecution to rely on the evidential brea th test despite an election for blood taking
place, it would have provided for such an o ccurrence, and that the appropriate place to
review circumstances such as the inability to collect a blood sample despite compliance
with procedure is Parliament.” That was in July 2012. Well, Parliament, through this
member’s bill, had already addressed it, and this bill was in the ballot.
I want to come on to the question of the Attorney-General’s opinion in respect of
whether or not this bill actually breaches th e New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. I would
respectfully suggest that the person wr iting the opinion on behalf of the Attorney-
General is somewhat confused when he or she is describing that the effect of the bill
“would therefore be that the results of some positive evidential breath tests, that would
not otherwise be admissible in evidence, w ould then become admissible.” I think they
are confusing the word “admissible” with the word “admitted”. The evidence is
admissible, and, indeed, if blood is not elected, would be valid  evidence before a judge.
However, the law prevents it from being admi tted into evidence, and I think that is a
subtle but significant difference.
6628 Land Transport (Evidential Breath Tests) Amdt Bill 14 Nov 2012
The other part of the opinion of the Atto rney-General is that the presumption of
innocence does not apply in this case, and I would again respectfully challenge that. The
defendant, with whatever evid ence is presented before the judge or jury, is presumed
innocent in just the same way that, had blood not been elected, the breath evidence
would be admissible, and the presumption of  innocence would prevail. However, I do
accept that this is an issue for the select comm ittee to deal with when it comes before it,
and I hope that it does. I am sure the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee
under David Bennett will look at the issue very, very closely. I strongly support this bill.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: I think the previous speaker, Michael
Woodhouse, made a proper concession just now that this bill, the Land Transport
(Admissibility of Evidential Breath Test s) Amendment Bill, does need careful
discussion at the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee. I hope, given that the
two larger parties at least are supporting the bill to that stage, that it will get that careful
scrutiny and discussion. I see that the chair of the select committee is here and is
listening to the debate, so I think the House can have that confident expectation.
The bill, in the name of Scott Simps on—and I congratulate him on his good fortune
in having it drawn from the ballot—aims to cure what I think he concedes is a very
small number of cases where unusual events conspire to prevent a blood specimen being
taken, and the example that I think has been us ed in a number of the speeches to date is
the one where there was a person who was addicted to drugs and had compromised
veins. The current situation is this. A br eath result cannot be used as evidence once a
blood test has been elected by the person who ha s been stopped at the side of the road,
or at a checkpoint or what have you, for that purpose. The bill would provide that breath
tests can be used if a blood specimen was not  able to be taken from the defendant, and
the words of the bill are “for any reason”.
I think the concern that I would want to put on the record is the breadth of the
expression “for any reason”. I think people can s ee that it is a useful thing to try to plug
a loophole, but I think that what we do need to  do is make sure that we do not, as in the
old clichéd proverb, use a sledgehammer to cr ack a nut. What I woul d not want to see
by passing the legislation, if that is the ultimate fate of the bill, is the legitimising of a
failure by the police to take effective acti on to ensure that there was a blood taker
available in circumstances where the legisl ation would set out th at expectation. The
problem that I have, just on my reading of th e bill, is the breadth of the expression “for
any reason”. It is very wide. It would in clude there being no blood taker on the roster
that night. I know, and I know that other members in the House know, that police go to
a heck of a lot of trouble at the moment to make sure that they can comply with the law.
They do go to great lengths with their roster s to make sure that there is somebody who
can take blood if that is the election that the driver on the scene makes.
Let us remember that these safeguards  exist for good reason. The breath test is
generally pretty reliable, but we know that there are cases where that has not proved to
be the case. We should also remember that random stopping is an innovation in our law.
It is an exception—and it was a controversial exception at the time it was introduced—
to the principle that there ought  to be reasonable cause for a seizure or search. We have
seen the benefit of this innovation, because we have seen the road toll come down. So
we all support it. But we want to make su re that the safeguards remain. We want to
make sure that what we do not do is inadve rtently give the police, who are pressured
always for resources, some opportunity to cut corners by, for example, saying: “Well,
we don’t need to have a taker of blood on th e roster, because we’ve got this marvellous
exception that Scott Simpson has given us, and it means that for any reason we can
ignore that requirement.”
14 Nov 2012 Land Transport (Evidential Breath Tests) Amdt Bill 6629
I just wanted to make that contribution in  my speech. I think the policy of this bill
makes a lot of sense, but we do not want to invalidate the entire regime that Parliament
has carefully put in place over a number of years—breath te st then blood test, but the
blood test as a proper back-up in the case that it is need ed—to protect liberty and to
ensure that people going about their lawful bus iness are not subject to penalties. So in
order to support this legislation further, past the select committee, the Labour Party
would need to see, at the very least, that matter considered and resolved appropriately.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I thank members for the many
considered contributions to the debate from both the Labour and National sides of the
House. First of all, I would like to co mmend the proponent of the Land Transport
(Admissibility of Evidential Breath Tests) Amendment B ill, Mr Scott Simpson. As a
member from the Waikato region as well, I know Scott and he is a very, very loyal
constituent member who has done a great j ob for his people, advocating for them time
and time again and delivering results for his el ectorate. I think they are very lucky to
have such a high-calibre member, and I thin k his exceptional degr ee of dedication and
devotion to his electorate will shine through in  future elections. So that is very, very
good. I also commend Mike Woodhouse, our whi p, who did a great job in putting this
idea forward in an earlier stage, but—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: What about Phil Heatley?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Oh, I do not know about Phil Heatley, actually. But Mr Simon
Bridges? Yes, that Minister is  going to help us through this process. He is an excellent
Minister, as well.
I think it is pretty obvious what the bill is trying to  do, and members of the House
have talked about it. I know that Phil might need it said again so that he can grasp it, but
it is not that hard. There are some issues around how it will actually be done. That is the
case with members’ bills. Often we put a bill forward, and the process of getting official
advice and of letting member s discuss the content of the bill through the parliamentary
process in this House and through the select committee process is vital to make changes
and get the bill right. I would like to th ank the Labour Opposition for supporting this
bill going forward so that we can go through that process and we can have a look at it.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Unlike that side. They don’t support our bills.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I see Darien Fenton over there. She is one of those very strong
and very effective Labour members of the Transport and Industrial Relations
Committee, along with Phil Twyford and Andr ew Little. We look forward to their
working constructively, as they normally do in the committee. It is a very good select
committee, actually. We have very cordial relations in the committee. We have efficient
and timely meetings, and we deal with issues of great importance.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: What about the rail submissions? The Gisborne to Napier line?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Now we are getting New Zealand First. Those members
always have to cause trouble. They cannot s it quietly in a debate like this. I guess there
is a conspiracy theory about this bill, ac cording to the New Zealand First mantra of
politics. So what is the problem with it?

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: It’s actually the first sensible bill we’ve heard from that side for
quite some time.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: It is the first sensible bill. Are they voting for it? That is going
to be the question. That will be the issu e. Whether they can vote Yes will be another
question.
I do want to congratulate members of the committee on the way they work together,
and I think they will undertake to work in that way on this bill. Scott Simpson is
actually a member of the committee, and a very fine member as well. I think he is going
6630 Land Transport (Evidential Breath Tests) Amdt Bill 14 Nov 2012
to have a lot of questions tomorrow at the committee meeting. I think his important
role—

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: He better read the bill, then.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: —yes—on the committee as the proponent of the bill means he
will take an active interest in how it passes through the political and legislative process.
I guess that, in the sense that we have alwa ys wanted to see the safest and strongest
roading system that we can have, it is impor tant that we make these changes where and
if necessary to look after public safety. The No. 1 thing that members of this House are
entrusted to do in regard to these kinds of bills is to make sure we look after our young
people and our drivers and take the approach of trying to do the best we can so that we
do not have issues where people try to game th e system or take advantage of it, and so
that there is a fair and equitable system out  there that applies for all. Those are the
words that New Zealand First members should listen to—“fair and equitable”. They are
words that your leader holds dear, but to you as a party I say that we look forward to
you supporting this bill, because it is fair and equitable. Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Is the member calling?
Denis O’Rourke: I am calling, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I did not hear you.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : That was probably because of the noise coming
from the other side of the room. Anyway, I wo uld like to say this in response to what I
have just heard. In fact, yes, New Zealand First does support the Land Transport
(Admissibility of Evidential Breath Tests) Amendment Bill. We think it is a common-
sense approach and, yes, we do think it is fair and equitable. It is fair to say that. We do
think, in particular, that there is a defect in  the Act as it is at present, where a positive
evidential breath test is not admissible simp ly because the suspect person has elected a
blood test but is in circumstances where no blood test is possible. That is a defect. It is a
hole in the legislation and it does need to be fixed.
New Zealand First is very much in support of  all practical means to make sure that
such loopholes are closed and that people who are, in fact, guilty of drink-driving are
caught. Provided that that is done with due pr ocess of law, then we think we should be
as tight as possible in maki ng sure that all such people are, in fact, prosecuted, and
prosecuted successfully. It is just not good enough that somebody should be able to
elect to take a blood test knowi ng, in fact, that a bl ood test is unlikel y to be possible,
and then to be in a position where their breath test is not admissible.
I would have to say, though, that I do not thi nk that the drafting of this particular bill
is very good at all. In fact, the provision—

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Grammatically incorrect.
DENIS O’ROURKE : Well, that is true. My friend Mr Horan has said that it is
grammatically incorrect, and it is poor gramma r. It says in clause 4(2): “After section
77(4), insert: ‘(5) Subsection (3 )(b) does not apply if a bloo d specimen was not able to
be taken from the defendant for any reason.’ ” What kind of grammar is “was not able
to be taken”? I do not know who wrote this, but they need  to go back to school and
learn some grammar. But, more particularly, we need good drafting of this bill. The bill
should be amended so as to read, for exam ple: “Subsection (3)(b) does not apply if it
was not possible or practicable for a blood sp ecimen to be taken …”. That is what I
presume it means, and if that is what it is intended to mean, that is actually what it
should say, not these poorly drafted words that we see before us.
When we see members’ bills coming forward in this way, people should at least take
the trouble to draft them properly, so that not only is the English correct but also it
actually says what it is intended to say. I th ink that the word “possible” or the word
“practicable” is what is intended, so we want this to be amended. We want to see that it
14 Nov 2012 Land Transport (Evidential Breath Tests) Amdt Bill 6631
covers only situations where it is actually not  possible to get a blood test or where it is
not practicable to do so. So we would expect to see this amended accordingly.
Another thing that it shoul d do is this. The last few words are “taken from the
defendant for any reason.” That is not good enough, either. That is also poor drafting,
because what we do not really mean is “any reason.”, and what we should do is tighten
that a little bit as well. I think it should say, for exampl e, “unavoidable reason.”, or
words to that effect.
New Zealand First, if it going to continue to support this bill in the future, would like
to see that it is properly drafted and amended accordingly. But I would like to go on and
say this: drink-driving remains one of New Ze aland’s most serious safety issues, and I
do not think we are doing nearly as much in this country as we should about it. This is a
very small measure. It is worthwhile, but we  would expect of the Government that it
takes a lot more action on controlling drink-driving.
The new amendments to the alcohol bill will take us a little bit further in respect of
that, but we also need to take further acti ons in respect of who may drive a car. Driving
a car is a privilege and there must be furt her restrictions on doi ng it, especially in
relation to people who are affected not just by alcohol but also by any situation in which
their driving ability is impaired.
So we would like to see much more compre hensive legislation than we see here. In
particular, we need to address much more the behaviour of people who drink
excessively. We need to be tougher with the penalties—much tougher than we are
now—and we need to widen the scope of offences that already exist.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: It gives me a huge pleasure to speak
in favour of the Land Transport (Admissib ility of Evidential Breath Tests) Amendment
Bill. May I congratulate the initiator of th is bill, Scott Simpson, the member for
Coromandel. This is, indeed, a—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: It was Woodhouse who drafted it.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: Well, maybe it was. So there is another Government
member to congratulate on this very good bill. I am also pleased to be standing to the
right of the chairman of the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee, David
Bennett. I know that he will very ably en sure that the bill goes through the select
committee very expeditiously.
But I want to just go back in history a b it of time to when I was a young medico and
the days even—believe it or not—before accura te breath testing. On the North Shore
there was a very infamous doctor. What we used to do when the drivers were brought in
was have them firstly undergo the “walk along  the line straight” test. They were then
asked a few questions, and if they failed both, they would have the choice either to have
their blood taken for testing or to be put in to the cell. The very infamous doctor was
infamous because he was not good at getting blood. I vividly remember going in when I
was a locum for him one day, and this guy had anticipated and said that he would go for
the cell, thanks. But he was very relieved to see me and said: “Look, I feel a little bit
embarrassed now that I’ve opted for a night in the cell. If I’d known you were on—you
are pretty slick at taking blood—I would have opted for the blood test, and it would
have saved me the night.” However, the re levance is this: today we do have pretty
accurate breath testing. Of c ourse, if someone opts against having an evidential blood
test as well, then I think it is quite right and proper that the breath test is, indeed, taken.
There is the issue of those who have bad vein s, and it is quite true that some number
do have bad veins, whether they are those who take drugs all th e time or, perhaps,
someone on dialysis therapy. I can think of Joeli Vidiri, the great rugby player, who,
sadly, is on dialysis treatment and has just  about no vein in his body for a blood test
6632 Land Transport (Evidential Breath Tests) Amdt Bill 14 Nov 2012
other than the jugular. Quite clearly it would be  inappropriate to take a blood test if that
was relevant in that case.
So we see here a bill that is elegant in its  simplicity and absolutely relevant in terms
of the mechanism for the remedy to forgoi ng the blood test when someone opts not to
have it. I can say that I am delighted to support it. I hope, indeed, that New Zealand
First members, who sounded as though they we re wavering a little bit a moment or two
ago when I—

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: No, there was never a waver.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: They are not wavering? That is good. There is definitely
support coming from New Zealand First, and Mr Horan can guarantee that his party will
be supporting it. I am very glad to hear that. This is an excellent bill. Scott Simpson is to
be congratulated. I certainly commend it to the House.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It is a great pleasure to be
concluding this first reading debate on my Land Transport (Admissibility of Evidential
Breath Tests) Amendment Bill. As various speak ers in the debate have indicated, this is
not a bill that is going to have an impact on a particularly large number of people, but
the people it will have an impact on are curr ently able to literally evade the provisions
made by this House in the principal Act rega rding drink-driving, a nd they are literally
able to get off scot-free.
I want to thank members for their considered debate, for their contributions to the
debate so far. I am very much looking forw ard to participating in the select committee
process, under the capable a nd very able chairmanship of  David Bennett. I know that
once we get it to the Transport and Indus trial Relations Committ ee we will address
some of the issues that have been raised in the debate so far. I wa s particularly pleased,
early on in this exercise, to receive from  Mike Noon of the Automobile Association
support in principle from that organisation. It  too understands that there has been a very
significant attitudinal change towards drin k-driving in this nation over the last
generation or so, since Dr Hutchison was practising medicine as a young intern some
years ago—

items.speaker: Dr Paul Hutchison
items.text: Just a few years ago.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: —just a couple of years ago—and things have changed a little
bit. Society’s attitude towards those who drive while under the in fluence has changed
significantly, and for even a small number of peop le to be able to evade the intention of
this House in bringing them to remedy for the consequences of their poor social
behaviour—and, indeed, their illegal driving—I think is a matter that needs addressing.
I want to spend just a minute referring, for the sake of those members who did not
hear it in the original speech, to the judgment relating to the case of Police v Childs
heard in the Rotorua District Court just this year—in fact, in July of this year. Judge
MacKenzie examined all the current case la w and had to dismi ss the case against
Childs. He had blown a screening test—that is the one where you have got the little
electronic device, where you have to give your name and address—and he proved
positive on that. He then blew an evidential breath test, and then was given the option of
a blood test, which he was perfectly entitled to take under the existing law. However,
Mr Childs was an intravenous drug user of  some long number of years and his veins—
he knew, I suspect—were utterly unable to be tapped for the required sample of blood.
So after 40 minutes—40 minutes—of attempti ng to draw a signifi cant and appropriate
blood sample, the medical officer was not able  to do so. When the case came before
Judge MacKenzie he had to throw it out because the situation of the facts presented
meant that Childs was statute-barred from being prosecuted, because no blood sample
was available to him.
14 Nov 2012 Land Transport (Evidential Breath Tests) Amdt Bill 6633
I think that is wrong, and even  if it is for a small number of people each year, it is
still wrong, and for this House not to addre ss what was actually an oversight in the
original legislation—in the original 1998 legisl ation—I think is something that we need
to turn our attention to now. Thus the measure of the bill.
I want to thank the originator of the bill, my colleague the senior Government whip,
Michael Woodhouse, who did indeed draft the original bill. I am sure I can vouch for
his grammar and the accuracy thereof. He has a good education.
The Attorney-General’s report is something that is worth a small consideration
because the report does sit on the Table of this House. But like other speakers on this
side, I respectfully reject the position that the Attorney-General has taken on this matter.
It will still be the case of the police, as in any criminal matter in our criminal
jurisdiction, to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. That  is the measure of all
criminal convictions in New Zealand, and nothing would change under my bill. The
Automobile Association, in its support of the bill, has indica ted that it too would like to
consider narrowing the clause a wee bit, a nd that is a matter that will be rightly and
properly addressed at the select committee. I am looking forward to participating in the
process. I thank members for their consider ation so far, and commend the bill to the
House.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Land Transport (Admissibility
of Evidential Breath Tests) Amendment Bill be now read a first time.
Ayes 105
New Zealand National 59; New Zealand Labour 34; New Zealand First 8; M āori
Party 2; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Noes 15
Green Party 14; Mana 1.

CONSERVATION (NATURAL HERITAGE PROTECTION) BILL
First Reading

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I move, That the Conservation (Natural
Heritage Protection) Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Local Government
and Environment Committee to consider the bi ll. There are several populations of very
attractive jewelled geckos on Banks Peni nsula and also a population on the Otago
Peninsula. They are attractive to us becau se they are the most wonderful creatures—
green, with yellow and white markings. They are pretty unique as well, giving birth to
live young and also being active during the day. These geckos, endemic to the South
Island of New Zealand, are highl y protected and it is illegal to disturb or capture them.
Unfortunately, jewelled geckos are also attrac tive to wildlife smugglers, who, if they
can get them past our borders, can make an extraordinary amount of money from them.
Smugglers come to New Zealand often posing as tourists. Some of them are acting as
agents for overseas collectors, and have maps and global positioning system points
provided by overseas syndicates , with the detailed locati ons of where to find our
geckos. They might hire a campervan and they  might visit, and then revisit, the same
site on the Otago Peninsula or Banks Penins ula over a number of years, targeting our
iconic species over and over ag ain, and literally ripping off our heritage. The smugglers
are driven by the big money that they can ge t at the huge trade fair s overseas, held in
Europe. These trade fairs are where our nativ e wildlife, such as jewelled skink, are
6634 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 14 Nov 2012
openly sold, and if you go on the internet, which is easy enough to do these days, you
can see pictures of them in plastic contai ners like Tupperware or GladWare containers,
sitting there on perhaps a paper towel, and they are easily identifiable by way by their
markings, which are pretty individual to them.
So they are openly sold, both on the internet  and also at these large trade fairs,
reaching prices often of more than $10,000 each and more if it happens to be a pregnant
female. Just recently, a pregnant female was caught in the hands of a potential smuggler
at our border in Christchurch. She was pre gnant with two young inside her. I do not
know the price of that female, but the loss to New Zealand and to the native population
is a—

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: Priceless loss to New Zealand.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Well, it is a priceless loss to New Zealanders and is pretty keenly
felt by those of us who are neighbourly w ith these skinks in  Otago and, indeed,
Canterbury. For the Otago population of je welled gecko, poachers are now a larger
threat than even cats and ferrets, and it is estimated that the population has been
decimated by up to one-third over a period of  5 years, leaving a population of fewer
than 5,000 in Otago.
The Wildlife Enforcement Group, which wa s set up by the Government, is doing
wonderful work. It is based in the Customs Service, toge ther with the Ministry for
Primary Industries and the Department of Conservation. In 2010 a German gentleman,
Manfred Bachmann, was caught in Christchurch by the Wildlife Enforcement Group
with 16 jewelled gecko in a backpack on hi s person. He pleaded guilty to being in
possession of absolutely protected wildlife under the Wildlife Act and was sentenced to
15 weeks in jail, and, in my view, that is not enough.  The Conservation (Natural
Heritage Protection) Bill does not only apply to the jewelled gecko, of course. Plenty of
New Zealand’s precious and pr otected flora, fauna, and na tural and historic resources
are under threat. The new penalties proposed in  the bill, relating to animals, will also
cover the poaching and smuggling of tuatara and of parrots. Some penalties in the
current legislation are far too low. Upon sentencing German national Manfred
Bachmann, who was found guilty of smuggling jewelled gecko, Judge Farish, who was
presiding, noted: “Given the va lue of these creatures, perh aps the penalty needs to be
increased to deter you and other people from thinking it’s appropriate to come here and
steal these valuable creatures from our c ountry.” I could not ag ree more with those
sentiments.
This bill proposes amendments to the Conservation Act 1987, the National Parks Act
1980, the Reserves Act 1977, the Wildlife Act 1953, and the Wild Animal Control Act
1977. Instead of a sentence of 15 weeks in jail for smuggling jewelled gecko, the likes
of Mr Bachmann would face up to 3 y ears’ imprisonment and a fine of $200,000.
Maybe that would send a strong message to  him and his like in the international
smuggling community, and they will know that they are not welcome here in New
Zealand with their smuggling ways.
The bill not only increases penalties for offences but also provides a consistent
approach across a number of Acts. Under the bill, fines for reserves and national parks
will come into line with each other and will provide clarity across the main regulations
administered by the Department of Conservation.
The message we want to send people thr ough this legislation, should it be passed, is
that New Zealand is not, should not, and w ill not be a soft touch for overseas smugglers
coming to New Zealand to steal our natural heritage. So this bill sends a strong message
that we take the protection of New Zealand wildlife and our natural areas very seriously.
We New Zealanders pride ourselves on our clea n, green image. It is imperative that we
look after our natural environment, because  it is our greatest asset. A consistent
14 Nov 2012 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 6635
approach to penalties across the laws admini stered by the Department of Conservation
will ensure appropriate and effective penalties, punishment, and enforcement.
I want to finish my contribution toni ght and my introduction to this bill by
commending the commitment and the work of the Department of Conservation. I also
want to commend the commitment and the work of the Customs Service and also those
personnel in the Ministry for Primary Indus tries in their work with the Wildlife
Enforcement Group, and I hope that this bill wi ll give them more teeth. I commend the
bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: I acknowledge the member who has
just resumed her seat, Jacqui Dean, and sa y that her presentati on of her Conservation
(Natural Heritage Protection) Bill was s poken with some insight and passion, and I
commend both. I am very pleased to say that Labour is supporting this bill.
Mrs Dean said she wanted to see better protection of New Zealand’s wildlife and
natural and historic resources, and she talked about the jewelled gecko on Banks
Peninsula and Otago Peninsula. As the member of Parliament who used to represent
Banks Peninsula before it was stolen unkindly from me by the Hon Amy Adams and put
into the Selwyn electorate, I was privileg ed to see those geckos on a number of
occasions and I really enjoyed them. I know th at a former Minister of Conservation, the
Hon Dr Nick Smith, was part of those experi ences, as well, when he was not kayaking
in Akaroa Harbour, waiting for a reserve to be  put there. The reserv e still is not there,
Dr Smith, so get back in that job and let us get it progressed.
I remember not very long ago having a bill that made quite a small amendment to the
Resource Management Act, but it was one that in my view was quite significant because
it changed the part of the Resource Management  Act that allowed for private enterprise
to compulsorily acquire land in order to  progress their projects. I thought it was
something that really deserved cross-party support in the House. I remember the Hon Dr
Nick Smith’s contribution in that debate—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: They’re always memorable.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Perhaps my colleague Grant Robertson is correct—they are
always memorable. I certainly remember this one because he said that we should not do
little bits of changes, even though the bill wa s a member’s bill. He said we should look
at the whole issue—we should look at a comp rehensive approach. He was talking about
the Resource Management Act. So I am looking forward to Dr Smith’s speech tonight
when he, with the same consistency of princi ple, refuses to support his colleague Jacqui
Dean’s bill, on the basis that it is not even a tinkering. It is not worthy of even the
description of tinkering. It is such a small amendment. But it is significant. It is very
comparable to the Resource Management Act amendment I introduced, which Nick
Smith railed against and then led the vote agai nst. So whilst supporting this bill, I look
forward to his contribution, because I will  be giving him marks out of 10 for his
consistency and I would like him to score highly on that point.
This bill ensures that not only are the penalties for, as the member described, trying
to smuggle our precious gecko etc. out of th e country, or releasing pests into natural
reserves, which is another one  of the penalties, increased but actually they are made
more consistent, and I think that is a very good thing. At the moment, if someone
released a stoat into a nature reserve, the highest penalty they could receive would be a
$500 fine or 1 month’s imprisonment. That in itself is quite bizarre because $500 does
not seem all that much actually but 1 month’s imprisonment seems like quite a lot. So I
think there is some inconsistency within even the existing penalty regime. Under the
National Parks Act, if part of a national park is carved off and converted to pasture, or
to a stand of trees that then is mille d, the highest penalty is $2,500 or 3 months’
imprisonment. So there is quite an inconsis tency between those offences. But if those
6636 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 14 Nov 2012
same offences happened in a conservation area such as the Ka imanawa Conservation
Park, the maximum penalty for the same offences would be $10,000 or 12 months in
prison. So, again, how did all of  this come about? Well, it  came about because we did
not have an overview in the way that the member has provided for in this member’s bill.
And we know that the areas that national parks protect are typically of higher value than
conservation areas, so it is even more foolish.
So while Labour will be supporting this bill, and I certainly look forward to the
debate at the Local Government and Environment Committee, if that is, indeed, where it
is referred to after the vote, I have to say that  out of all of the thi ngs that are happening
in the conservation space, I would have thought that a member of the Government
might have used the opportunity of a membe r’s bill to make sure that the fundamental
role of the Department of Conservation was secured and perhaps even—it might be a bit
dramatic for the National Party—enhanced, not just left as the status quo. The Hon Nick
Smith’s eyes are lighting up, because I know that is what he would want to do with it;
not just retain the status quo but strengthen th e role of the Department of Conservation.
What we have seen over the last 4 years is a real dumbing down of the department. I
think that is a huge shame and it is something we will pay for over the longer term,
quite significantly.
The National Party sees the environment a nd the economy as separate entities that
need to be balanced, rather than seeing them as dependent on each other, or two sides of
the one coin, which is the way Labour sees  those issues. So the Department of
Conservation has lost its place as a critical player in our public policy. We do not have
the advocacy role. We certainly do not ha ve in the Minister an advocate for
conservation issues. We saw the Minister ju st stand back and watch Gerry Brownlee
and Steven Joyce bowl over her views in term s of mining of schedule 4 land. It was not
really until thousands of New Zealanders go t on the street and pr otested against the
possibility not of mining—the protest wa s not against mining—but of mining in our
most special places, the pieces of land that are protected under schedule 4 of the Crown
Minerals Act. Those pieces of  land are there for a particular  reason, and they should be
protected. That is why they are put under schedule 4 of that legislation.
We know that the Department of Conservation has had massive staff cuts. During the
submissions on the Game Animal Council Bill we heard a lot about the relationship the
Department of Conservation has with local pe ople in provincial area s in particular. In
some parts of the country the Department of Conservation works alongside recreational
hunters, works alongside iw i, works alongside community groups, works alongside
schools, to make sure that those conservati on values are seen as  part of the ongoing
resources and win the support of the communit y. But what we have seen in other areas
is that, through the staff cuts that the National Government has imposed on the
Department of Conservation, th e staff have been centralised, they have been moved to
other parts of the country, and those relations hips are just not po ssible. There are not
local people doing that job any more. We know that over the next 12 months we are
going to see further staff cuts in the Department of Conservation.
One of the areas that are of most concern is the lack of scientific research that is now
available as a core function of the Departme nt of Conservation. If we want evidence-
based research, if we want best practice, if  we want to be really confident that the
decisions made in regard to conservation are made on the basis of evidence and on the
basis of good information, we need that scie ntific base. We have seen good scientists—
some of the best scientists—leave the Depa rtment of Conservation because the work is
not there for them. Even when there is some work available, they do not get the
satisfaction any more of knowing that that work is going anywhere.
14 Nov 2012 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 6637
I hope that the Minister of Conservation, when it comes to the next big decision that
she has to make, is able to get some cour age, which she has not demonstrated in many
recent decision-making processes. That deci sion is in regard to protection for M āui’s
dolphins. The submissions have closed just this week, and thousands of New Zealanders
put in submissions calling for protection of the most endangered dolphin, and a dolphin
that is New Zealand’s dolphin. There are only 55 adult M āui’s dolphins left. I implore
the Minister to use her power as Minister of  Conservation and to not be pushed back by
the people in her Cabinet who do not care nearly as much about our dolphin or our
reputation internationally as they do about so-called economic benefits. There is a
bottom line, and I think that the future of a species that we are responsible for protecting
should be a big part of that bottom line. I wa nt the Minister respons ible for fisheries to
put some money into sustainable fishing prac tices for New Zealand, so that instead of
the fishing industry losing out in a decision to protect the M āui’s dolphins, we can get a
win-win situation. But at the moment th at is not happening. The Minister of
Conservation is standing by and letting th e Minister for Primary Industries run the
place. I think that is a great shame.
The conservation values that we have in New Zealand are importa nt to us. This bill
will give us an opportunity to make better sens e of our penalty regime, but also to give
better protection to some—

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I am very pleased to
support the Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill in the name of Jacqui Dean.
I would like to congratulate Jacqui Dean  on having two bills in the House this
afternoon. It is great work, and she is a hard-working member for Waitaki.
I think we are all concerne d that New Zealand’s unique plants and animals are at
risk, and we want to be able to protec t them better. Our plants and animals are
exceptional. They are totally unique, highly desirable, and greatly prized, and a real
temptation to the collectors of the world, who are always looking for the unusual, the
beautiful, and, particularly, the unobtainable. Unfortunatel y, there are many collectors
globally who are happy to pay big money for these creatures. They will pay for the
skinks, for the geckos, for our birds, and,  really, for anything that is unique and
different, and that comes from the other side of the world. We have also seen a dramatic
increase in violence against creatures, as well as the poaching, the stealing, and the
smuggling. New Zealanders all find these be haviours abhorrent, be cause we are proud
of our country, we are proud of our plants, birds, and reptiles, and we want to make sure
that they stay here. We want to protect our natural spaces and the birds and creatures
who live in them.
This bill introduces bigger fines and l onger jail sentences for people who endanger
our wildlife or damage our protected natura l habitats. We need to have a consistency
across the 5 Acts amended by this bill. It was interesting that the Hon Ruth Dyson
mentioned the lack of consistency. That is wh at this bill is drivi ng at: consistency and
penalties that deter unacceptable behaviour. We  are serious about th is. We are serious
about deterring this type of crime. It is not  just a crime against our  flora and fauna; it is
also a crime against the people of New Zeal and. So we are introducing a maximum fine
of $10,000 or a 2-year jail sentence for offences conducted in both reserves and national
parks.
I was horrified to find out that collectors fr om Asia and from Europe are particularly
interested in our unique  reptiles, particularly creatures like the jewelled geckos that, as
Jacqui Dean has mentioned, live in Banks Peninsula and Otago. These fetch enormous
prices overseas, I have heard, of up to $25,000 each. They are actually relatively easy to
catch in the remote parts of New Zealand, a nd they are quite easy to  transport as well.
Dozens of endangered lizards disappear from their native habitats every year. Many are
6638 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 14 Nov 2012
in the hands of suspected organised criminal groups, who sell them on the internet. New
Zealand geckos are particularly prized, because  they give birth to their young live, so if
you get a pregnant one, you actually get a whole lot of free geckos as well.
In the past 3 years seven people have b een caught smuggling protected geckos and
skinks out of the South Island. One group, in cluding a German from Uganda who was
sentenced to 15 weeks in jail, was caught with 16 jewelled geckos. They were packed in
tubes; others put them down their pants or in their clothing. But these 16 geckos were
valued at over $200,000, and at least nine of  them were pregnant. The geckos usually
end up on a German website, wher e traders claim that they ha ve been bred in captivity.
It is not true, and it is not right. I know that the Department of Conservation and
Wildlife Enforcement Group are working very hard to protect these geckos and skinks. I
support this bill, because it does show how seriously we are taking these issues and how
much we value our birds and reptiles. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call
on this Conservation (Natural Heritage Prot ection) Bill. As othe r speakers have noted,
there is a lot to be said positively about this bill in the sense that it takes seriously the
issues that have been raised about smuggli ng and about protecting our flora and fauna,
by increasing fines and trying to address some  of the inconsistency within the various
fines regimes that cover our conservation esta te, and that cover the flora and fauna that,
as the previous speaker, Nicky Wagner, has said, we are all so proud of in New Zealand.
It always strikes me when we look at legi slation that is about fines and regimes for
penalties that we find ourselves in the H ouse continuously trying to update them like
some kind of inflation index here within the House.
I do wonder at the wisdom sometimes of legi slation that sets do llar figures and then
expects time to stand still and those dolla r figures to somehow mean something. As
Ruth Dyson said earlier, when you have a situation where it is a $500 fine or 1 year in
prison, that indicates that time has got away on the legi slation. I do think that overall
there is a question of whether it is wise to be setting in legisla tion particular dollar
figure penalties when, in fact, what we are tryi ng to do is express the will of Parliament
about the seriousness of these offences—whe ther, actually, we are better off with some
other kind of system that does not require us to come back as some  form of inflation
index every few years and make the changes that are being proposed  tonight by Jacqui
Dean. But that is obviously not in the scope  of this particular bill, and the fines
increases and penalty increases that are indicated in the bill seem to me to be
reasonable. Certainly, from the Labour Party’s point of view, we are keen to see this bill
go to the Local Government and Environment Committee to discuss the wisdom of the
penalties regimes as they stand.
But if we are talking about making things c onsistent, there is one thing that we can
say that is absolutely consistent about this Government’s approach to conservation
matters, and that is the fact that from th e day its members entered office, they have
undermined the operations of the Department of Conservation—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: That’s rubbish!

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Dr Smith says it is rubbis h. Let us go through the record.
The 2009 Budget cut $54 million out from the Department of Conservation—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Over how many years?

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: —with 400 job losses, Dr Smith. That was projected just
in 2009. Dr Smith ask over how many years. It does not matter, Dr Smith. Taking $54
million out of the budget of the Department of  Conservation undermines the work. It is
all very well for National members to come to this House with bills that look like they
care about the conservation esta te and that improve the pe nalties regime, but sitting
behind that is a cut of $54 million from the Department of Conservation.
14 Nov 2012 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 6639
In September last year they  announced that they were cutting 96 members of staff at
the Department of Conservati on. That is staff from 12 c onservancies right around the
country. Members of this House will know as they travel around the country the impact
of those cuts on those local conservancies. It is not like it was the great back-office cuts
that we were told about. These are peopl e in regional New Zealand who are charged
with protecting our conservation estate whom  this Government has cut. These people
include the scientists. As Ruth Dyson said before, what the department needs is the
ability to be able to provide the informa tion for the evidence-base d decisions that Dr
Smith and others would tell us that they be lieve in. But it is those scientists who have
lost their jobs under this Government.
The Government has systematically underm ined the Department of Conservation,
and what we are now left with is a situation where only 250 of 2,700 threatened species
are actually under active management.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: Remind me the relevancy to the bill?

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Louise Upston asks how this is relevant. What is the point
of a penalties regime that involves the conservation estate if the Government
undermines the very protection of that estate, and of the protection of the flora and
fauna that this Government says it cares a bout? It puts the penal ties regime up, but the
department that is charged with looking af ter it is consistently undermined by this
Government. Now we have a department re liant on private donations and groups to fill
in the gaps. It is great to see corporations  getting behind things like kiwi recovery, but
in the end, if the BNZ decides it has got other pr iorities, there is nothing left inside this
department. We support this bill to the select committee, but we do so knowing that this
Government has a record of undermining conservation.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Deputy Speaker. I am pleased to take a
short call on the Conservation (Natural Herita ge Protection) Bill. I congratulate Jacqui
Dean on bringing this bill to the House, b ecause it increases and implements a much
more consistent approach to penalties for offences that are committed under the
Conservation Act, the National Parks Act, th e Reserves Act, the Wildlife Act, and the
Wild Animal Control Act. One of the areas where it does this obviously is by increasing
the penalties for offences under this conservation legislation for the smuggling of native
wildlife. That is why the Green Party will  be supporting the bill, because the existing
penalties have not increased for some time, and they are out of step with the prices that
are being paid internationally for wildlife th at is smuggled out of Aotearoa and then
sold internationally. There has been a range of court cases where it is quite clear that the
existing penalties of up to a $100,000 fine and 6 months in jail are not providing a
deterrent. So we are pleased that the bill will increase the offending penalties where it
has been done by individuals for commercial purposes, or by a company—and that is a
higher penalty than for offending by an individual.
But I am also somewhat bemused by this bi ll, because it is a member’s bill, yet in
September the Minister of Conservation said that the Government would be introducing
the Wildlife (Smuggling Deterrence) Amendment Bill later this year, and the object of
that bill was to increase the maximum pena lties for smuggling wildlif e such as tuatara,
parrots, and geckos—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Conspiracy—there’s something tricky going on here!

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: So yes, Mr Bridges, what is going on here? Because the
Minister, when she announced the intention to introduce that Government bill, said that
the penalties would be increased to up to 5 years’ imprisonment and/or a $300,000 fine.
So I would be interested in the comments fr om the member Jacqui Dean in reply about
what happens when the Government does in troduce the bill that has been promised.
How does this bill improve on what the G overnment and Cabinet had already agreed,
6640 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 14 Nov 2012
and is it potentially duplicating that? Nevert heless, we welcome the bill and we will be
voting for it.
As other speakers on the Opposition benches have highlighted, this is a good bill, but
the Government is not investing adequate ly in conservation. We have seen a $54
million cut to the Department of Conservati on’s budget, and in the annual report of the
department released in September, it showed  that there were 114 fewer front-line staff
in 2011-12 than in 2009-10, and a total of 181 fewer permanent staff. That reduction in
front-line staff gives the lie to the Government’s promises and claims that its slashing of
the public sector budgets is not reducing people on the front line.
Of course, it is the people on the front line—the Department of Conservation staff
who are out maintaining tracks and huts, controlling wildings and willows, doing
predator control, and providing advice to hunters, trampers, and international visitors—
who are the front line against smuggling, because it is often those staff and members of
the public who are alert to susp icious activities. People go to visit the quite compliant
sites and habitats where species like the jewelled gecko are found and then alert the
wildlife enforcement group and warranted officers, who can step in and take action. So I
pay on behalf of the Green Party enormous tribute to those front-line Department of
Conservation staff, particularly in area offices, who are being threatened by their
substantial second round of restructuring, which means that they are all going to have to
apply for their jobs.
It was a senior investigator in the wild life enforcement group who described wildlife
smugglers as “greedy people without any consid eration for animals”. That is certainly
true where these people are snatching speci es like the beautiful  jewelled gecko from
their habitats, stuffing them in small plastic containers, and taking them overseas. It is
these lizard fauna, particularly distinctive species like the jewelled gecko, which have
been targeted because of their bright gree n colouring and that very unusual diamond
pattern. Of that species, there are only about 5,000 individuals left, and they now
confined to small areas of Otago and Canterbury, particularly on the peninsulas. Habitat
loss and predation have affected them, and poaching is a huge impact and has caused
several of the populations to crash. So the Green Party supports th is bill increasing the
penalties for those individuals who are taking these geckos out of their habitat.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I think we are all pretty familiar with
the very unique range of flora and fauna that exists only in these islands of New
Zealand, and that makes us particularly vu lnerable to those from overseas who would
like to steal either our tuatara, our geckos, or  the wide range of bird species that exist
only in New Zealand. We have seen some high-profile prosecutions against people from
various parts of the world who have tried to profit out of those pretty ugly crimes, and it
is appropriate that this Parliament is c onsidering a bill to up both the fines and the
criminal sanctions against those people invol ved in those crimes. I want to join with
others and commend Jacqui Dean, a member  of Parliament for one of the most
spectacular parts of the count ry, with both South Canterbury and North Otago in that
Waitaki area. I think her practical passion for conservation is what typifies this
Government’s blue-green approach of wanting to be pro jobs and pro the economy, and
wanting to be a successful, innovative countr y, but at the same time wanting to ensure
that we look after that which is precious.
I want to respond to a couple of the cha llenges that have come from members
opposite on this bill, the Conservation (Natural  Heritage Protection)  Bill, firstly, from
Green MP Eugenie Sage. She questioned the auth enticity of this bill on the basis that
the Minister of Conservation, Kate Wilkins on, who is doing a great job, had said that
this was an area that needed  to be addressed. Somehow the Green MPs are concerned
that a Government MP has taken the init iative and picked up on the work and the
14 Nov 2012 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 6641
comments that have been made by Kate Wilk inson. Well, we are a team. Yes, we have
Ministers doing some pretty good work in this space, but we also have strong and
capable backbenchers who are complementing that work with this sort of bill. Equally
so, we have had the tired, ol d rhetoric from a couple of Labour members saying “Hey,
this is a great bill, but National’s not spe nding nearly enough on conservation.” Well, I
say that is a bit tired. Do they not know that this Government faces huge economic
challenges, and that there is no way that  anybody could sensibly promote the ongoing
increases in public spending?
I was on the Finance and Expenditure Comm ittee this morning, and this morning we
had the Secretary to the Treas ury and Audit New Zealand no ting that the huge increase
in expenditure—a 50 percent increase in public expenditure—on core departments in
the period from 2002 to 2008 was totally unsust ainable. It is absolutely true that
whether it is the Department of Conser vation, or right across the board, this
Government has had to pull in Government e xpenses. That is why it is so unfair and
uncharitable of members opposite to give the Mi nister of Conservati on a hard time for
pulling her weight and doing her share to get this country’s books back in balance.
The challenge I have got for the next Labour member is this: if you really are serious
about increasing the conservation budget, you need to say by how much and you need
to say how you are going to fund it. These hollow words, where I have had
spokespeople right across the Labour benc hes—I do not care whether it is on
broadcasting, heritage, conservation, educat ion, health, or forei gn affairs—all say the
Government is not spending enough. My simple challenge to members opposite,
whether it be in conservation or  any other area, is to show us the colour of your money,
say it with conviction, and commit a future  Labour Government to increase levels of
spending, rather than these weasel word s of “Oh, you’re not spending enough.”, but
then not being prepared to commit to how much you would spend. It is not good enough
for Labour members not to say how they would fund their increases in expenditure. This
bill from my colleague Jacqui Dean is part of this Government’s sensible conservation
agenda. She should be commended and this bill should be supported.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the honourable
member Charles Chauvel.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: Well, it might be pronounced a bit differently,
but it is nice to have the call. To try to ma ke a response to the challenge laid down by
the last speaker, the Hon Dr Nick Smith, this is a bill, the Conservation (Natural
Heritage Protection) Bill, that has rightly attracted support across the House. It is a
sensible bill and I commend Jacqui Dean for her initiative in putting it forward.
The question of whether it is an appropriate member’s bill  or whether it ought to be
something that the Government advances as part of a technical review of penalties
available in the conservation and related legi slation, in order to make sure that those
penalties work as part of a coherent regime , is another question. I have said before, as
have other members, that the thing about member s’ nights is that they are special. They
are there for members who are not part of th e executive to be able to advance matters
that they feel passionately about, that ca nnot otherwise be part of the parliamentary
agenda. I am not belittling the bill by saying that it would be the sort of measure that we
would support if it was part  of a Statutes Amendment B ill, rather than taking up the
time of a members’ night. So I think that is the first point that I want to make.
The second point that I want to make is a direct response to Dr Smith. I want to say
this: Dr Smith, it is not about splashing money around, actually; it is about commitment.
Everybody knows that you have a commitment to  the environment. I have never heard
anybody in this House question your deep belief that the New Zealand natural
6642 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 14 Nov 2012
environment is one of our treasures. I have heard people speculate about the extent to
which your colleagues share that belief, and I think that is fair speculation.
I have also heard people say—and I think this is right—that we should look at the
record. I am very proud of this party’s record on environmental and conservation
matters. The fourth Labour Government, unde r Geoffrey Palmer, marked our first
Minister for the Environment, who held a statutory warrant in that post, which was
revolutionary in this regard. Yes, th e Environment Act 1986 was Sir Geoffrey’s
brainchild, as was the Conservation Ac t 1987. All the groundwork that was done to
ensure that the Resource Management Act could be enacted was done under his
leadership. And New Zealand’s first steps to respond to the challenge of climate change
were taken under that administration, as well.  That is an extremely proud record that
every member on this side of the House wants to associate themselves with.
Technical reforms of this nature that bring penalty regimes into line with one another
are all well and good, and of cour se we are going to support them. As I say, I am a little
concerned that the Government is taking up the time of the House on a members’ night.
We could be spending time on non-Government members’ passionately held beliefs that
they seek to advance via the member’s bi ll process, but never mind. Every member has
the privilege that Ms Dean is exercising tonight, and she has chosen to exercise it in this
way.
But what has to be said, what has to be re peated, is what has been said by a number
of Labour members and by Eugenie Sage, and th at is this: if you want to talk about
record, Dr Smith, then this Government’s record on conservation and the environment
is poor. It is extremely poor. If we look at the cuts in spending in the Department of
Conservation right through to the decisi on to abandon the Kyoto Protocol second
commitment period so that there are no bi nding commitments to reduce emissions, and
at all the public policy failures to bring about a change in our economy and in our
society so that we really do start to act sustainably and renewably—that is the tragedy of
this Government. That is the tragedy that we see in this minor measures bill, which is
praiseworthy and will be sent to a select  committee, and no doubt will pass through all
its stages, but it is tinkering. It is tinkering around the margins of the issues that matter.
As I say, if we want to talk about records and want to take up the challenge laid down
by Dr Smith in the earlier contribution, that is the sad reality of life under National.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I take a call on behalf of New Zealand First on
the bill brought before the House by the member Jacqui Dean, the Conservation
(Natural Heritage) Protection Bill. Can I congratulate her on having two bills in the
House on the one day. Should she pull another bill from the ballot today, I think she
should be shouting us all, because it is excepti onal to have two bills in the House in one
day. We are all heading off to Christch urch in the morning—that is, the Local
Government and Environment Committee, including Jacqui Dean as a member—and
she might be shouting coffee in the morning, at the Wigram airbase, I hope.
But back to the bill. We in New Zealand Firs t certainly do also support this bill. It is
high time that the penalties were increased for those who offend in terms of our flora
and fauna, our wildlife and nature, and that th e penalties are made to such a significant
level that, hopefully, it might deter some of the illegal acti vities that have been going
on.
It is pleasing to see, in section 44, in clause 5, that the penalties will increase for
individuals “to imprisonment for a term not exceeding 2 years and to a fine not
exceeding $100,000, and, where the offence is a continuing one, to a further fine not
exceeding $10,000 for every day on which the offence had continued;”. Where the
offence was committed by an individual for commercial purposes the penalty is
“imprisonment for term not exceeding 3 years and to fine not exceeding $200,000, and,
14 Nov 2012 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 6643
when the offence is a continuing one, to a further fine not exceeding $20,000 for every
day on which the offence has continued;”. Where the offence was committed by a
corporation the penalty is “a fine not exceeding $200,000 and, where the offence is a
continuing one, to a further fine not exceeding $20,000 for every day on which the
offence has continued.” It is also pleasing to see in this bill that a sentence of
community work can be imposed where someone has erred and where perhaps a
financial fine is not appropriate. Again, we in New Zealand First support that.
We believe that the amendments in th is bill to the Conservation Act 1987, the
National Parks Act 1980, the Reserves Ac t 1977, the Wildlife Act 1953, and the Wild
Animal Control Act 1977 are necessary to bri ng that in to line. However, there is a
downside to all this, and although we ar e applauding the move to increase these
penalties, we concur with some of the other members in this House that at times we are
very lax with our conservation. As the cons ervation spokesman for New Zealand First I
also have concerns, and our party has concerns, at aspects of conservation that are being
let down in this country. We are so, so de pendent on our natural environment for our
tourism and for the image of New Zealand as “100% Pure New Zealand”.
Our conservation estate is extremely important, and it flows on into our agriculture, it
flows on into our horticulture, and it flows on into other farming aspects in this country.
So if we do not have a healthy natural e nvironment, our commercial agricultural and
horticultural environment can be affected as well. So it is very important that the two go
hand in hand.
Likewise, this week I was somewhat di sappointed when it was marked that the
Māui’s dolphin, which are endangered, ar e nearing extinction, with only 55 M āui’s
dolphin left, mainly off the North Island coas t. I thought that perh aps the Government
would also pick up that cudgel, as it has picked up this one, and move more swiftly on
the issue of the M āui’s dolphin. I was one of the four  MPs who went along to receive a
print from artist Sheyne Tuffery, presented by Greenpeace. It was one of 55 prints to
mark the 55 remaining Māui’s dolphin that are in existence.
It was a great shame that only four MPs were there, all from Labour, the Greens, and
New Zealand First, and that there was no repr esentation at all from National. I thought
that was a shame. Regardless of your politics and regardless of where you are, these 55
Māui’s dolphin cannot speak up for themselves, they cannot defend themselves, and
they cannot protect themselves, and it woul d have been nice on this occasion for some
Government members to at least show some sympathy for the whole thing.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: I don’t think we were invited.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: Yes, you were invited. Every MP was invited—every MP
was invited. So it would have been nice, because I think it is important, and I think we
would all have a huge conscience to bear in years to come if we found that the M āui’s
dolphin was indeed wiped out and that every on e of us in this House, every single 121
of us in this House, had not done more to try to protect it.
But, anyway, in closing, this  particular bill is a good move. We support the increase
in penalties. New Zealand First always suppor ts things of this na ture where they are
good policy, practical policy, and will have a result. Thank you.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: It was interesting to have the reference from the
previous speaker, Andrew Williams, about  the National members not turning up. I
certainly read a bout that in the  Dominion Post  this morning. It was saying that the
National members had not responded to the invitation to be gi ven something on the
Māui’s dolphin. I went and dug around, and I found the letter, and there was no such
invitation to me—that is for sure. There was a letter saying something was happening,
but there was certainly no invitation. So you sometimes wonder with some of the
messages coming from Greenpeace, whether they are quite accurate or not.
6644 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 14 Nov 2012
But I just wanted to commend my colle ague Jacqui Dean for this bill, the
Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection)  Bill, her second bill this evening—a very
hard-working, and implacably hard-working, member of Parliament is Jacqui Dean. It is
a timely bill, because we all know New Zeal and is unique in the world as the last
significant uninhabited land mass in the worl d to be discovered by humans only a few
hundred years ago. I have seen trees growi ng today that were around before humans
arrived in these islands. I have seen trees  on which moas have grazed, which are still
living now, that were around before humans re ached these islands. As a result of that,
we were a wonderful, wonderful place in the world with all sorts of species that were
unique and had evolved over a long period of  time when New Zealand was splendidly
isolated from the rest of the world and fr om humanity. All that changed a few hundred
years ago when M āori arrived first and there was a wa ve of extinctions, and that has
continued in recent years—and that is only a split second, of course, in geological time.
We are in a time of rapid change, so it is important that we preserve what is precious.
This bill, which raises some of the maxi mum penalties in this area around precious
species, is very useful. I have never met a spotted or jewelled gecko. I do not understand
the logic of people who would seek to put th ese down their underpants, but from what I
can understand, this thing goes on. This bill, if it helps nip it in the bud, I think will be
very useful not just in New Zealand but to the global effort against smuggling of geckos
and those sorts of things.
New Zealand makes a massive effort in cons ervation. It is often forgotten that about
33 percent of the land mass of New Zealand is in the conservation estate. That is not a
mistake—33 percent. One third of the land ma ss of New Zealand is in the conservation
estate. We spend colossal sums on cons ervation—$445 million in  Vote Conservation
this year—and I am astounded to hear from th e other side of the House tales of great
woe and calamity that somehow not enough res ources have been put into this area. I
mean, let us just cast our minds back only 10 years ago, when it was only $226 million
that was being spent on conservation. So we  have doubled the amount  spent in the last
10 years, and that, of course, is not enough.
It is quite right, things have had to be pulled back a little bit in the last few years, but,
if you take the longer stretch, there is a very  substantial and increased investment in
conservation. It all just goes to show, when  you hear the likes of  Mr Chauvel talking
about the fact that we need to just keep  pouring the money in, how this country got
itself into such a pretty pass as we had in 2008, when this Government inherited a
nation pregnant with years of financial deficits coming down the line, because the
previous Government just did not have cont rol over its spending. I get frustrated when
hearing this great moral high gr ound taken from the other side of the House, as if those
members care more about the environment than we do.
What we are saying here is that every G overnment has to make that balance between
giving New Zealanders the be nefit of a well-run economy th at can produce the living
standards that all families want and aspire to  and also the very substantial contribution
that continues to be made in conservation. I am very proud of this Government’s record,
and I commend Jacqui Bill for this conservation bill, which will—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Jacqui Bill?

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: Jacqui Dean, I believe. I commend Jacqui Dean for her great
effort with this bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: I will take just a short call on the Conservation
(Natural Heritage Protection) Bill, in the na me of Jacqui Dean. I think it is a fantastic
bill, to see this increase in penalties ar ound the stealing and the smuggling of native
wildlife and plants. It has got particular meaning for me because, unlike Mr Goldsmith,
who spoke previously, I am familiar with the jewelled gecko. I remember watching
14 Nov 2012 Conservation (Natural Heritage Protection) Bill 6645
them—but not in my underpants —and seeing them in their natu ral habitat, at that point
in the Nelson Lakes. We are not sure that th ey even exist in any numbers in the Nelson
Lakes now, because the numbers have gone back so much. It is absolutely critical that
